Ex-TMC MLA Nirmal Ghosh arrested for ‘hastily cremating’ RG Kar rape-murder victim
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari had ordered the Barrackpore Police Commissioner to conduct a fresh probe into the alleged hasty cremation.
Former Trinamool Congress MLA Nirmal Ghosh was arrested in Odisha on Thursday in connection with the alleged "hurried cremation" of the doctor who was raped and murdered at Kolkata's state-run RG Kar Medical College and Hospital in 2024, police said.
Ghosh, who represented Panihati, was arrested on charges of destroying evidence, criminal conspiracy and forcing a person to carry out an act against their will, news agency PTI reported citing police.
The arrest came after the victim's father filed a fresh complaint at the Khardaha police station on Monday. He alleged that Ghosh was one of three people who had forced the "hurried cremation" of his daughter's body.
Bengal CM ordered fresh probe
West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari had ordered the Barrackpore Police Commissioner to conduct a fresh probe into the alleged hasty cremation while attending a memorial programme for the victim in Panihati on Sunday.
"The role of Ghosh, Dey and Mukherjee in the cremation needs to be investigated. I have ordered the registration of a new case separately, apart from the court-monitored Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). I have asked the Barrackpore Police Commissioner to take necessary steps in this regard," he had said on August 8.
RG Kar rape-murder case
The 31-year-old postgraduate trainee doctor was found dead in a seminar room at RG Kar Medical College and Hospital on August 9, 2024.
Investigators later found that she had been raped and murdered the previous night.
Police said her body was taken to a crematorium in Panihati, where it was allegedly cremated in haste after being moved ahead of two other bodies waiting in the queue.
The BJP government in the state has also been raised over the signatures on the documents granting consent for the cremation. Police said the signatures were allegedly those of neighbours rather than the victim's parents or other family members.
The CBI is separately probing the rape and murder case after the investigation was transferred from the Kolkata Police. One person has been convicted in the case, which is still pending before the Calcutta high court.

Over 2,950 free-ranging dogs (FRDs) were sterilised with the aim of saving Black-necked Cranes (BNC) and boosting wildlife tourism-based livelihoods in Ladakh under the initiative of Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) along with the Indian Army, the Animal Husbandry Department, and the Department of Forest, Ecology and Environment.
The initiative started in 2022 to conserve BNC chicks, after the wildlife expert noticed that FRDs have been killing them in the Alpine Wetlands of Ladakh and preventing BNCs from settling down in one place for nesting.
BNC, globally listed as “vulnerable”, is a cultural symbol and state Bird of Ladakh, but fewer than 100 survive in India, while the estimated world population is roughly 11,000–12,000 individuals, most of which occur on the Tibetan Plateau. They are distributed across four range countries—India, Nepal, Bhutan, and China.
According to BNHS authorities, 110–130 individuals are recorded annually, including 20–25 breeding pairs, depending on the year. The main breeding sites include the Changthang Cold Desert Wildlife Sanctuary, the wetlands of Hanle, Tso Kar, Nyoma, and nearby marshes, with an extended population in the Suru Valley. “During the annual population monitoring conducted in early June 2026, a total of 19 pairs of BNC were recorded across the wetlands of Ladakh,” said Kishor Rithe, Director of BNHS.
However, BNHS scientist Dr Muhammad Raza, working in Ladakh, informed that the actual number of pairs is expected to be slightly higher, saying, “Due to logistical challenges and limited accessibility, several sites could not be surveyed. BNHS is taking necessary measures to get a clear picture of the breeding population of BNC in Ladakh.”
Efforts under the initiative
BNC has been facing threats across its breeding habitats due to increased human use of areas surrounding wetlands, expansion of linear infrastructure, habitat degradation, FRDs, and the impacts of climate change.
To address disturbance to nesting birds at the hands of FRDs, BNHS led the initiative, which also includes efforts to reduce the availability of anthropogenic food subsidies. A pilot waste-management project has been initiated at selected Indian Army outposts to improve the handling and disposal of food and kitchen waste, thereby limiting access to food resources that sustain FRD populations.
“By integrating waste management with sterilisation efforts, the programme seeks to provide a long-term and sustainable approach to reducing dog-related threats in ecologically sensitive wetland landscapes,” said a BHNS authority.
Additionally, capacity-building and awareness programmes have been launched, and 1,000 armed forces personnel have been trained in biodiversity conservation and wildlife management.

India finished fourth at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, which concluded last week on August 2, with 39 medals — 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze. The result came despite the absence of several sports disciplines that have historically supplied the bulk of India’s Commonwealth haul, marking another chapter in a medal history that has grown from one medal in 1934 to 603 across editions.
India’s Commonwealth success has long been concentrated in a handful of sports. Shooting, wrestling and weightlifting alone account for 390 of India’s 603 medals, roughly two-thirds of the total. While boxing, badminton, and table tennis have added another 113.
Shooting, wrestling, badminton, table tennis and hockey, all important contributors to India’s past medal tallies, were absent. Glasgow hosted a pared-down programme of 10 sports after the Commonwealth Games was forced to find a replacement host following Victoria’s withdrawal. The 2026 programme included athletics, swimming, track cycling, weightlifting, 3x3 basketball, lawn bowls, netball, artistic gymnastics and judo and boxing, alongside para events.
Even without many of its traditional medal-producing sports, India still finished fourth.
A brief history
India’s Commonwealth journey began in London in 1934, when wrestler Rashid Anwar won India’s first medal, a bronze in the 74kg freestyle category and a 12th-place finish. India missed the 1930, 1950, 1962, 1986 editions, won no medals in 1938 and remained unranked in 1954. Its first gold medals came in 1958, when Milkha Singh won the 440-yard race and wrestler Lila Ram triumphed in the 100kg category, and Lachmi Kant Pandey won a silver.
The tally steadily grew, reaching 10 medals in 1966, 12 in 1970 and 15 in 1974, when India finished sixth each time. By 1990, it had risen to 32 medals and fifth place.
Women gradually became a larger part of India’s medal haul. Their first Commonwealth medal came in 1978, when badminton players Ami Ghia and Kanwal Thakar Singh won bronze in the women’s doubles at Edmonton. India then won two women’s medals in 1994 and three in 1998.
The breakthrough came in 2002, when the tricolour began to rise on the Commonwealth stage. India crossed the 50-medal mark for the first time, winning 69 medals and finishing fourth. It followed that with 50 medals and another fourth-place finish in 2006. Then came its greatest Commonwealth campaign at Delhi 2010, where India won a record 101 medals — 64 by men, 36 by women and one in a mixed event — finishing second.
In Glasgow 2026, India won 39 medals and women accounted for 41% of India’s tally.
The longer-term trend puts Glasgow in perspective. India accounted for just 0.5% of all medals awarded in 1934, when it won its first Commonwealth medal. Its share crossed 5% for the first time in 1990, when it won 32 of the 638 medals awarded. The share rose sharply from 2002 onwards, reaching 7.7% in 2002 and 6.7% in 2006. At the Delhi 2010 Games, India reached its peak, winning 101 of the 828 medals awarded —12.2% of the total. Its share remained above 7% in 2014 and 2018, at 7.8% and 7.9%, respectively, before falling to 7% in Birmingham in 2022.
In Glasgow, India won 39 of the 671 medals awarded, accounting for 5.8%. This was its lowest medal haul since 1958, when it won three medals. However, the smaller programme and the absence of several sports in which India has historically performed strongly make direct comparisons with earlier editions difficult. Overall, India won 603 of the 10,636 medals awarded across the editions in the editions India participated, accounting for 5.7% of the total.
Australia back on top
Australia finished first in Glasgow, returning to the top of the Commonwealth medal table after England topped the standings at Birmingham in 2022.
Australia’s dominance is also striking when viewed against India’s much larger population. It has accumulated 2,773 Commonwealth medals, compared with India’s 603, despite having a population of roughly 28 million against India’s 1.46 billion. Canada has won 1,709 medals with a population of about 41.7 million, while New Zealand has won 743 medals with just 5.3 million people.
The comparison is not intended as a medals-per-capita ranking — the countries have competed in different circumstances and across different numbers of Games — but it highlights the very different sporting systems behind their Commonwealth records. Australia has consistently converted a much smaller population into a far larger medal haul, as children have access to many sports, usually experimenting with multiple sports before finding their specialisation. Its nation-wide ‘Little Athletics’ is their initial introduction to athletics, equipped with experienced coaches, who are unrestricted by bureaucratic central bodies. Australian athletes aren’t pushed to perform young, and many gain experience in American colleges before competing officially. In contrast, India’s medals have historically been concentrated in a relatively narrow group of sports.

The BJP will shortly launch a protest across Dakshina Kannada and other parts of the State demanding the removal of B. Nagendra from D.K. Shivakumar’s cabinet, Dakshina Kannada district BJP president Satish Kumpala said in Mangaluru on Wednesday.
Talking to reporters, Mr. Kumpala said the Enforcement Directorate (ED) arrested Mr. Nagendra, who was the Minister for Scheduled Tribes Welfare Department, for his active participation in a conspiracy to siphon off ₹89.93 crore from the Karnataka Maharshi Valmiki Scheduled Tribes Development Corporation Ltd. The ED found evidence of the use of these funds for the campaign in the Telangana Assembly election.
Mr. Kumpala said despite assurances by Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar of zero tolerance for corruption, he had brought Mr. Nagendra back to the cabinet. The BJP and Janata Dal (Secular) will raise the demand for the removal of Mr. Nagendra from the cabinet during the proceedings of the two Houses of the State legislature, which begin on Thursday. The legislators of the two parties will not take part in the proceedings until Mr. Nagendra is removed from the cabinet. The State BJP president has already announced statewide protests demanding Mr. Nagendra’s removal.
“We will shortly announce the dates of protests to be held across Dakshina Kannada,” Mr. Kumpala said.
Asked about the statement by Mr. Nagendra that he was targeted because he comes from a Backward Classes community, Mr. Kumpala said the minister faces a serious charge of siphoning off nearly ₹90 crore. He cannot take shelter behind his community to evade accountability for such a serious charge.
Tiranga Yatra
A Tiranga Yatra was held in Puttur, Mangaluru, Mangaluru City South, and Sullia Assembly constituencies. Legal hurdles have been cleared and the yatra will be held in Kalladka in Bantwal taluk on Thursday. It will be held in Belthangady and Mangaluru City North Assembly constituencies on Saturday. The yatra will be held in Moodbidri Assembly constituency on Sunday, Mr. Kumpala said.

“Chennai is not just a metropolis; it is a living museum of culture, temples, and traditions that breathe beauty into modern life. A vast trove of history where the past merges seamlessly with the present. Citizens keen on heritage should visit the Tamil Nadu Police Museum, housed in the erstwhile Commissioner’s Office built in 1856 — a project I am proud to have been associated with,” said A. Amalraj, Greater Chennai City Police Commissioner.
“From Marina’s waves to IT corridors, the city balances timeless values with cutting‑edge progress. It embraces newcomers with open arms, offering unique opportunities to grow and excel,” he said.
“As Police Commissioner, my mission is to ensure peace, safety, and justice — protecting every citizen, every street, every dream. Each day brings unique challenges to the men and women in uniform, and the public’s cooperation with our new initiatives remains unparalleled. The city’s strength lies in its youth. Empowering them with awareness, discipline, and opportunity is our greatest investment. Yet, making citizens alert to new‑age crimes remains a real challenge. It is a real honour to serve this metropolis — safeguarding its legacy, nurturing its future, and celebrating its spirit,” he added.

Vice President C.P. Radhakrishnan on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) said the national song Vande Mataram played a crucial role in awakening patriotism among Indians and uniting people across regions, languages, faiths and social backgrounds during the freedom struggle.
Addressing the 'Har Ghar Tiranga' bike rally commemorating 150 years of Vande Mataram at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, Mr. Radhakrishnan said the two words "Vande Mataram" had "lightened the burning patriotism in the minds of every Indian in those days", becoming the prime force that uprooted the British colonial Raj from India.
"Our freedom struggle was an awakening of the Indian mind, the Indian spirit, and the Indian consciousness. It united people across regions, languages, faiths, and social backgrounds through a shared dream of freedom, a shared dream of one India," he said.
Mr. Radhakrishnan said when Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay penned the immortal words, he "gave voice to the soul of the nation wanting to breathe freedom".
"For our countless freedom fighters, this song was more than just words. They were a source of courage, sacrifice, and hope," he said, adding that many freedom fighters went to the gallows with "Vande Mataram" in their hearts.
Referring to the special discussion held in Parliament on the 150th anniversary of Vande Mataram, Mr. Radhakrishnan said the deliberation lasted more than 12 hours and was "one of the most engaging and meaningful deliberations of the session".
He said it was particularly significant for him as it took place during his "very first session as the presiding officer of Rajya Sabha".
Recalling his recent visit to the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Mr. Radhakrishnan said he visited the place where Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose had hoisted the Tricolour in 1943 and proclaimed the islands free from colonial rule.
Mr. Radhakrishnan said he also visited the Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Island and the historic Cellular Jail, where several freedom fighters were kept in solitary confinement.
He said many of the brave inmates of the Cellular Jail walked to the gallows singing Vande Mataram. "Their courage and sacrifice continue to inspire every generation of our country," he said.
"Vande Mataram is a call that transformed love for one's motherland into a national duty," Mr. Radhakrishnan said, adding that the sentiment spread "like wildfire from Bengal to every nook and corner of Mother Bharat".
He said India was now "marching confidently towards the vision set by our Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Viksit Bharat by 2047".
The 'Har Ghar Tiranga' bike rally was particularly meaningful as, in the 150th year of Vande Mataram, "we are taking the spirit of that song back to the streets", the Vice President said.
He said the country was now witnessing the fifth edition of 'Har Ghar Tiranga', which was launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in 2022, and the initiative has become "a people's movement".
"The strength of the Har Ghar Tiranga movement lies in the fact that the nation is not asking citizens to watch a celebration. It is inviting them to be a part of it," he said.
Citizens across the country were participating in Tiranga yatras, bike and cycle rallies, cultural programmes and concerts, he said, adding, "Each activity has a different form, but the sentiment behind them is common. The national flag is the symbol in which every citizen can find a sense of longing."
Union Minister of Culture and Tourism Gajendra Singh Shekhawat, Union Minister for Social Justice and Empowerment Virendra Kumar, Union Minister of State for Science and Technology Dr. Jitendra Singh, Union Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju, and Union Minister of Coal and Mines G Kishan Reddy were among those present.

Former Union Minister and Home Secretary R.K. Singh has sought answers from Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on how many patrolling points the Indian government has given up since 2014. He made these claims citing a recent report that Indian forces have allegedly abandoned a patrolling point called Shera 5 in the Taksing area of Arunachal Pradesh.

In a video post on X on August 12, 2026, former MP from Bihar’s Arrah parliamentary seat, Mr. Singh said, “I spent eight years in the Ministry of Defence and seven years in the Ministry of Home Affairs. I read a report today which gives me worry, and it should worry all the citizens of our country. It appears that we have abandoned a patrolling point called Shera 5 in Taksing in Arunachal, and the Chinese have established a prominent position there.”
Mr. Singh, who has become vocal against the government following his suspension from the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in November 2025, then explained what it means when patrolling is abandoned.
“The Chinese and us, have a dispute about the borders, and that dispute has been carrying on ever since the Chinese occupied Aksai Chin. The 1962 war was about that; the Chinese do not accept the McMahon Line as a border. They are also not willing to demarcate the Line of Actual Control (LAC) because they have huge claims into our territory, including the entire Arunachal Pradesh.”Mr. Singh said.
He added, “Now, because of these totally differing perceptions about where the border is and where the Line of Actual Control is, we carry out patrolling. Our patrols go up to points along our perceived Line of Actual Control and Chinese patrols come up to patrolling points along their perceived Line of Actual Control.”
He pointed out that this patrolling shows a marker; it shows where our claim line lies, so when the negotiations do happen, our perception of the claim line is very clear. That’s why patrolling up to these points is essential, so that our claim line is specifically communicated to the other side. Mr. Singh added that that’s the reason the Chinese also patrol to points along with their claim.
Mr. Singh alleged that when you abandon a patrolling point along your claim line and the Chinese occupy that means you have given up your claim. He added that one patrolling point where India has given up the claim has been reported in the newspapers.
He asked, “I want to know; the nation wants to know how many other patrolling points the government has given up since 2014. Is this the only patrolling point which the government has given up and the Chinese have occupied? Or are there other patrolling points which this government gave up, patrolling points which were being patrolled where our patrols used to go before 2014?”
Mr. Singh sought answers from the government, asserting that it concerns the whole country.
“This also gives a message about how pusillanimous, I will call it, this government is, that it cannot stand up even to the claim of the country. The Defence Minister and Prime Minister need to answer how many patrolling points have been abandoned since 2014 because giving up the claim on any points is not possible without the approval of the Prime Minister,“ Mr. Singh said.
A former IAS officer, Mr. Singh joined the BJP in 2013 and repeatedly attacked the BJP leaders during the State Assembly election in November 2025. He even questioned the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) candidates and accused the Nitish Kumar government of a ₹62,000 crore power scam in Bihar.

In 1967, an American businessman went for an afternoon walk in the Cameron Highlands of Malaysia and was never seen again. No clear explanation ever surfaced — only theories, ranging from tiger attacks to Cold War intrigue. That man was Jim Thompson, who transformed the fortunes of Thai silk and brought an age-old craft back into the global spotlight.
Delhi-based textile design company RR Décor recently launched Thai luxury and lifestyle brand Jim Thompson at Decorgeous Lifestyle in Chennai, marking the label’s entry into the South Indian market. The collection includes furniture fabrics, cushions, throws, curtains and blinds, bedding, and tapestries.
Thompson moved to Thailand in 1945 while serving with the US Office of Strategic Services (OSS), the US intelligence agency, which later became the CIA. Stationed in Bangkok at the end of the Second World War, he was captivated by the country’s architecture and traditional crafts. Declining to return to the US after the war, Thompson decided to turn his attention to the dying Thai silk industry.
“He was so fascinated by the colour, the texture, the individuality, and the human touch of the artisans. Because it was all handloom and handwoven, he really put a lot of effort into it. He introduced many new techniques in weaving, styling, and design, and by the early ‘60s, Thai silk had become a globally accepted fabric. All the leading design houses at the time — Gucci, Pucci, and Dior were using it for evening gowns, bridal wear and couture,” says Rohit Khemka, founder, RR Décor.
The launch showcased a selection from Jim Thompson’s 2026 collections. Nirin highlights handwoven Thai silk in natural colours and textured finishes, while The Citadel by No. Thompson showcases the relationship between urban architecture and nature. Oriental Odyssey revisits motifs from Thailand’s Rattanakosin era in a collection of luxury fabrics and wallcoverings.
Ochre and gold dominate much of the collection. Among the standout pieces is Golden Fans, a silk-blend fabric featuring folding-fan motifs woven into a satin base with gilded threads. Inspired by the ceremonial fans of Thailand’s royal courts, it combines traditional symbolism with a contemporary aesthetic. Another one is Lost Kingdom, which reimagines Ayuthaya the ancient Thai kingdom; here, gilded details and architectural silhouettes of Siamese temples are showcased in a way that tells the story of a generation.
From the creative director of home furnishings for the brand, Dao’s reinterpretation of Jim Thompson’s signature oriental textiles, inspired by the temples and cultural heritage of East and North Thailand, to Bill Bensley’s Wild collection, which draws from his deep connection with wildlife and nature, the collection brings together two very distinct facets of Thailand.
“People often assume Chennai is a market that prefers only subtle designs, but that’s changing. People have travelled, they’ve seen the world, and they’re much more open to colour and statement pieces now. We wanted to bring that perspective here,” says Rohini Vasudevan, chief designer, Decorgeous Lifestyle.
With the latest launch in Chennai, the brand continues to draw from Thailand’s artistic and textile traditions, while giving it a contemporary touch.
The collection can be found at Decorgeous Lifestyle, Gandhi Mandapam Road, Kotturpuram. Priced at ₹30,000 onwards.

Rape survivors, with pregnancies up to 24 weeks, do not require the permission from a court to seek a legal termination of pregnancy, the Madhya Pradesh High Court has said.
A Single Bench of Justice Sandeep N. Bhatt in Indore on August 11 made the remarks hearing a petition filed by the father of a 16-year-old sexual assault survivor who sought the court’s approval for the girl’s 18-week pregnancy. The petition cited extreme mental trauma for the survivors to continue with the pregnancy.
Saying that the matter did not require court intervention, Justice Bhatt disposed off the plea while citing a February 20, 2025, verdict that the High Court’s Division Bench in Jabalpur had earlier clarified that under the provisions of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971, survivors of sexual assault, rape, or incest, with pregnancies up to 24 weeks, who want to undergo an abortion do not require judicial proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution.
The court also issued directions to State’s Health Commissioner to communicate the Jabalpur Bench’s judgement to hospitals in the State for future reference.
“The Commissioner, Health Department, may also communicate the aforesaid order passed by the Division Bench to all the concerned hospitals more particularly the Government Hospitals, so that they can also take care of the situation in future,” the Indore Bench order read.
“With the above directions, since no intervention is required in the matter, present petition is dismissed,” it said.
In February, 2025, the Division Bench headed by the then Chief Justice Suresk Kumar Kait had laid out standard operating procedures (SOPs) to be followed by concerned officials and medical officers while dealing with pregnancies of rape or incest survivors for both cases where the pregnancy is of less than 24 weeks and beyond it.
It had asked the authorities to not demand any legal or magisterial requisition or other documentation as a pre-requisite in cases with pregnancies up to 24 weeks, while saying that court’s permission was only required if the pregnancy is of more than 24 weeks.

The Erode Forest Division has asked the owner of an animal breeding farm in Perundurai to produce the registration certificate and other documents relating to two Lar Gibbons (Hylobates lar) found at his facility during an inspection by officials of the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB), Chennai, and the Forest Department.
K.V. Appala Naidu, District Forest Officer, Erode, told The Hindu the registration process for the animals was incomplete and the owner had been asked to produce the required documents on August 14. Though he had produced certain documents, there were some shortcomings. The documents sought included the registration certificate obtained by the Manipur-based owner from whom the animals were purchased, Mr. Naidu said. Details had also been sought regarding the death of a female Lar Gibbon that had not been reported to the authorities, as reporting such an incident is mandatory under the Living Animal Species (Reporting and Registration) Rules, 2024, he said.
The inspection of the farm owned by K. Keshavanathan followed a video posted on social media by Tamil film actor Vikram in which he was seen petting and hugging a Lar Gibbon. The video went viral and drew criticism from wildlife activists over the possession of an endangered species without the requisite documents. The actor later removed the video. The Lar Gibbon is listed in Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES).
What the probe found
The inquiry revealed industrialist C.K. Ranganathan of Erode had purchased two Lar Gibbons from the farm owner and moved them to Chennai. Mr. Ranganathan is the father-in-law of Mr. Vikram’s daughter. Further inquiry revealed that the farm owner had purchased the animals from Manipur and brought them to Perundurai.
Under the regulations governing exotic live species, an owner is required to register with the Forest Department, declare the stock in his possession, and report the acquisition of any new animal within 30 days. Only after the declaration is made will the facility be inspected by the Forest Department to verify compliance, following which a Form 3 Registration Certificate will be issued.
The animals arrived at Perundurai on June 5, 2025. However, the owner applied for registration only on August 9, 2025, and transferred the animals to Chennai on the same day. “There was a delay of more than two months,” Mr. Naidu said.
The DFO said the registration process remained incomplete and the Forest Department was examining the documents produced by the farm owner.

The computer did not create a virus. It did not touch a test tube or handle a living cell. What it did may ultimately be more consequential: it helped decide what the virus’s genome should be.
Researchers at Stanford University and the Arc Institute used artificial intelligence (AI) to design complete genomes of bacteriophages - viruses that infect bacteria. Of 285 AI-generated designs physically synthesised and tested in the laboratory, 16 produced functioning phages. Some were able to overcome bacterial resistance that defeated the original virus. The phrase ‘AI-created viruses’ therefore needs qualification. Humans have been synthesising viral genomes and deliberately modifying viruses for decades. What is new, is not the physical manufacture of a virus. AI has entered the design stage of biology. For medicine, that creates remarkable opportunities. For biosecurity, it raises equally important questions.
From reading genomes to designing them
Bacteriophages -literally “bacteria eaters” -have been known for more than a century and are among the most abundant biological entities in nature. In 1977, one particularly small phage, ΦX174, pronounced roughly ‘phi-X-one-seventy-four’, became the first complete DNA genome to be sequenced. By the early 2000s, scientists had shown that viral genetic material could be synthesised from known sequence information and used to recover functioning viruses. Humans had progressed from reading viral genomes to writing them. Scientists then became increasingly capable of deliberately altering viruses. The controversial influenza gain-of-function experiments of 2011-12 showed that genetic changes could modify important properties such as transmission in experimental animals. Such research highlighted a dilemma that remains unresolved: the same science that can improve pandemic preparedness may also create biosafety and biosecurity risks.
The Stanford-Arc experiment represents the next step. The scientists already knew the ΦX174 genome and already knew how to synthesise viral DNA and recover functioning phages. What changed was who -or what -proposed the genome. They used Evo 1 and Evo 2, genome language models. The principle resembles a large language model, except that instead of learning patterns in words, Evo learns patterns in DNA. It studies the genetic alphabet - A, C, G and T - across vast numbers of genomes and then generates new genetic sequences. For this experiment, the models were further trained on thousands of bacteriophage genomes related to ΦX174.
AI did not invent a completely unrelated virus from nothing: it generated previously unseen ΦX174-like whole genomes within a known biological framework. Scientists selected some of these sequences, physically manufactured the DNA and introduced it into E. coli. If the genetic instructions were biologically coherent, the bacterial machinery produced new phage particles. 16 designs succeeded. The progression is striking: we learnt to read viral genomes, then to write them, then to modify them. Now AI is beginning to help decide what should be written.
One finding shows why this matters. An AI-designed phage successfully combined a viral protein with other genetic changes in a way that conventional engineering had struggled to achieve. The significance is not simply that AI can propose individual mutations; it may increasingly be able to identify multiple genetic changes that work together across an entire genome, exploring combinations that would be extremely difficult for humans to test one by one.
The medical opportunity
The most immediate application may be phage therapy. Antibiotic resistance is steadily eroding conventional treatment options, while bacteriophages offer another way of killing bacteria. Their major limitation is specificity: a phage effective against one bacterial strain may fail against another, and bacteria can also develop resistance to phages. Traditionally, researchers have searched nature and phage libraries for suitable candidates or modified existing viruses. Generative biology introduces another possibility. Instead of asking only, “Can we find the phage we need?”, medicine may increasingly ask, “Can we design the phage we need?”
The Stanford experiment offered an early demonstration. Combinations of AI-designed phages overcame resistance in E. coli strains against which the original ΦX174 failed. For clinicians confronting antimicrobial resistance, this is potentially important. The possibilities extend beyond phage therapy. AI can assist the design of vaccine antigens, antibodies, therapeutic proteins and viral vectors used to deliver genetic treatments. It may eventually help optimise oncolytic viruses that selectively attack cancer cells. The larger revolution is therefore not simply ‘AI making viruses’. It is AI becoming capable of designing biological function.
The danger is acceleration
It is tempting to be reassured because ΦX174 is an exceptionally simple bacteriophage, while dangerous human viruses are vastly more complicated. Human pathogens must negotiate receptor binding, host range, tissue tropism, replication, immune escape and transmission. But complexity should not become false reassurance. Human scientists already understand much about these determinants. Decades of virology, reverse genetics and gain-of-function research have linked many genetic changes to viral behaviour.
AI does not need to rediscover virology. Its power lies in integrating what humanity already knows, examining vastly more combinations than humans can explore manually and accelerating the path from hypothesis to experimental design. This is the real biosecurity concern: capability amplification. The relevant question is not whether an untrained individual can ask today’s chatbot to generate a pandemic virus. It is whether increasingly capable AI could make a knowledgeable and well-equipped laboratory substantially more effective at designing biological systems.
Future systems may compress months or years of literature review, modelling and experimental planning into much shorter cycles. Combined with increasingly automated laboratories, that acceleration could become profound. Even the apparently modest success rate in the Stanford study deserves this perspective. Only 16 of 285 designs worked, but digital systems can generate enormous numbers of candidates. A low success rate is reassuring only while the number of attempts remains small. Biosecurity will therefore also have to evolve. Traditional DNA-synthesis screening often asks whether an ordered sequence resembles a known pathogen or toxin. In the age of generative biology, researchers increasingly argue that screening must also consider biological function: not simply whether a sequence looks dangerous, but what it might actually do.
Safety without paralysing science
AI companies are already confronting this dilemma. Claude Fable 5 was initially deployed with strong safeguards around biology, chemistry and cybersecurity. Legitimate scientific work could sometimes trigger a fallback to a less capable model. The intention was understandable, but the experience illustrated the problem: too little restriction creates risk, while too much restriction can obstruct legitimate science.
Those safeguards have since been refined to reduce false-positive biology fallbacks, while more sensitive capabilities remain restricted. This points towards a more practical model: graduated, auditable access in which legitimate researchers can obtain stronger capabilities under appropriate institutional and security controls. Biosecurity also cannot rest entirely on what an AI model agrees or refuses to answer. Safeguards are needed throughout the chain - AI systems, DNA-synthesis providers, laboratories and institutional biosafety oversight.
India must build capability
There is an important implication for India. If frontier AI becomes central to drug discovery, genomics, vaccines, protein engineering and experimental design, access to advanced AI becomes part of national scientific infrastructure. Smaller and specialised models will be sufficient for many tasks. But a country can choose to use a small model because it is sufficient; it should not be forced to use one because somebody else owns the frontier. If researchers elsewhere receive trusted access to highly capable biomedical models while Indian scientists depend on restricted public versions, the resulting disadvantage could accumulate across drug discovery, vaccines, antimicrobial resistance and other fields.
India is already investing through the IndiaAI Mission and indigenous foundation-model programmes. That ambition should include scientific and biomedical AI, secure compute, high-quality datasets and trusted-access frameworks for legitimate researchers. AI sovereignty without biosecurity would be reckless; biosecurity without AI sovereignty could leave us scientifically dependent.
Governing biological intelligence
The Stanford experiment does not show that AI can casually manufacture dangerous human viruses. It shows something more precise: computers are beginning to move from analysing biological information towards proposing biological designs that scientists can physically build. That capability could transform antimicrobial resistance research, vaccines and therapeutics. It could also accelerate harmful biological engineering. The answer is neither prohibition nor unrestricted access, but controlled acceleration -allowing beneficial science to progress while safeguards increase with capability and risk.
The challenge is no longer simply whether AI should be allowed to understand biology. It is how we govern AI when understanding biology increasingly becomes the ability to design it. India must be capable not only of regulating and consuming that revolution, but of participating in its science and helping shape its safeguards.

SC expresses concern over pendency of cases at NCDRC, bats for regional, circuit benches
New Delhi, The Supreme Court on Thursday took serious note of the pendency of cases in the National Consumer Dispute Redressal Commission and asked the Centre to consider setting up regional and circuit benches to clear the backlog.
The top court also called for performance audits of state and district consumer commissions. The forums should not become rehabilitation centres for retired judicial officers, it said.
A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked the Centre to consider setting up regional and circuit benches of the national consumer forum, saying a consumer must not be made to travel all the way to Delhi, instead, the forum must go to them.
The bench asked the chairman of the NCDRC to furnish a status report on total pending cases, total complaints filed, average rate of disposal of cases, estimated time likely for disposal of a pending case and need for increasing the strength of members of the commission.
The top court, which is monitoring the functioning of consumer commissions, including appointments, service conditions and infrastructure. said the report must be filed in two weeks.
The top court was informed that pendency of case is huge in NCDRC as the matters which are being taken up for hearing at present are from 2018-19.
While some lawyers informed the bench that if a matter is listed in June this year, then the next date of listing of the matter is almost next year while others said that 30-40 matters are normally listed in post-lunch session, which does not get disposed of.
The bench then told Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for Centre in the matter that if the arrears are piling up in the NCDRC, then the only option left is to increase the maximum strength of the commission.
"We have a consumer friendly jurisprudence and pendency of cases can be reduced by increasing the number of benches," CJI Kant said.
The top court, however, said the quality of orders passed by NCDRC, which come up in appeal before the top court are very good, which shows that the problem is with filling vacancies of members of commission.
It asked the amicus curiae in the matter to also furnish data on pendency in state consumer commissions, vacancies and the information about the oldest case pending in the commission.
The bench asked the state consumer commission to furnish evaluation reports of district consumer forums for the last three years and posted the matter after three weeks.
Last month, the top court said that states with fewer than 1,000 pending consumer disputes may abolish some district consumer forums and transfer those cases to regular courts with approval from the jurisdictional high courts.
"All those states where the total pendency is less than 1,000 cases shall be at liberty to abolish some of the district forums and entrust the cases to the serving judicial officers, with the prior concurrence of the jurisdictional high court," the top court had said.
The clarification came during the court's current exercise to ensure compliance with its earlier directions governing the constitution of state and district consumer commissions and the service conditions of their chairpersons and members.
In its February 11 order, the apex court had noted submissions from several smaller states, especially the northeastern states and Union territories, that maintaining separate consumer commissions despite very low pendency was financially unviable.
It referred to such states as Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Tripura, Mizoram, Manipur and Goa, as well as the UTs of Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where only a limited number of consumer disputes were pending.
The court also observed that some states did not have constituted state consumer commissions headed by a sitting or a former high court judge. The bench thus directed that pending matters from certain states be transferred to the registrars general of the jurisdictional high courts.
A single judge of the high court, sitting with the existing technical members, would hear those cases as a deemed state consumer commission, it then said.
In February, the top court also permitted states and UTs with fewer than 1,000 pending complaints and appeals to submit alternative proposals to ensure effective consumer dispute resolution.
It asserted that states with below the 1,000-case threshold may also rationalise their district consumer forums by transferring cases to serving judicial officers, provided the arrangement receives the prior concurrence of the concerned high courts.

The world’s only winged mammals, nocturnal bats, of which there are some 1,500 species globally, have never quite got great press. Superstition has them down as bad omens. And science implicates them as the possible origins of the COVID 19 pandemic that killed seven million people globally, and in the outbreak of several other zoonotic diseases (that is, diseases that hop between animals and humans), including SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) in China, MERS (Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus) in Saudi Arabia, Ebola in Africa, and Nipah in India.
So how do these animals, that have catalysed sweeping disease outbreaks among people around the world, not fall sick from the viruses they carry and transmit? Now a new paper in Science Advances untangles this conundrum.
Researchers studied the world’s largest family of bats, and found that they, unlike every single mammal in the world, possess two copies of genes that produce antibodies (proteins that help the immune system fend infections), and not just one.
“We’ve never seen anything like this in a mammal before,” said Hannah Frank, associate professor of ecology and evolutionary biology at Tulane University author of the study, in a release. This completely changes our understanding of mammalian immune systems "and raises exciting new questions about why bats have been so evolutionarily successful and how they respond to viruses,” he added.
For the study, the scientists looked at vesper bats, of which there are 500 species across the globe, except Antarctica. They studied the antibodies, which are protective Y-shaped proteins made of two heavy protein chains and two light protein chains. Unlike all other mammals, including humans, vesper bats have two separate heavy-chain gene systems, boosting their antibody diversity, they discovered.
To unravel the evolutionary origins of this duplication, the scientists studied genomes of 34 species of bats, including 26 closely related bats and found that the copy is present in every vespertilionid examined except the pallid bat, Antrozous pallidus.
How bats remain reservoirs of viruses without being infected by them could assist scientists understand immune responses among different species and help prevent disease spillover, said the paper. “It doesn’t fully explain why bats are such effective viral reservoirs, but it reveals a level of immune variety we didn’t know existed and gives us an entirely new direction to explore,” said Dr. Frank
In an older study, also published in Scientific Reports, researchers found that bats and coronaviruses have been evolving together for millions of years: this has produced different strains in different groups of bats around the world, it added. Scientists studied various coronaviruses in 36 bat species from the western Indian Ocean and nearby areas of Africa and found that different groups of bats had their own unique strains of coronavirus.
India is home to 135 species of bats, forming the largest order of mammals in the country, according to State of India’s Bats 2024-2025 published by the Bat Conservation International and Nature Conservation Foundation. Despite the critical role they play in ecosystems, by dispersing seeds, pollinating plants and preying on pest insects, “bats receive an insignificant amount of attention from the country’s research and conservation communities and scant recognition in government policies and programs,” this document said.

Vande Mataram or the National Song will be sung from the ramparts of the Red Fort in New Delhi for the first time on Independence Day, preceding the National Anthem. It is also the 150th anniversary of the adoption of Bankim Chandra Chatterjee’s Vande Mataram as the National Song. But the original adopted version included only the first two stanzas. Recently, the Centre notified that all six stanzas would have to be sung.
The Centre issued guidelines on February 11, 2026, for the rendition of the National Song at public gatherings, schools, and official government functions, among others. This comes after the passing of the Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Act, 2026, which amended the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. It is now a criminal offence to intentionally disrupt, obstruct, or prevent the singing of the Vande Mataram.
The duration of singing and specific directions for playing by a band, among other rules, have also been mentioned in the circular.
Vande Mataram to precede Jana Gana Mana
The circular mentions that the National Song Vande Mataramshall be played or sung before the National Anthem‘Jana Gana Mana’ on all occasions when both are to be played or sung.
Vande Mataram duration
The total duration of the National Song must be “approximately 3 minutes 10 seconds.”
If played by a band, it should be preceded by a “by a roll of drums to assist the audience to know that the National Song is going to be played, unless there is some other specific indication that the National Song is about to be played, as for example, when fanfares are sounded before the National Song is played.”
The circular adds that “the duration of the roll, in terms of marching drill, will be 7 paces in slow march. The roll will start slowly, ascend to as loud a volume as possible and then gradually decreases to original softness, but remaining audible until the seventh beat. One beat rest will then be observed before commencing the National Song.”
Vande Mataram: Occasions for rendition
- Civil Investitures
- On arrival of the President at formal State functions and other functions organized by the Government and on his departure from such functions
- Immediately before and after the President addresses the Nation over All India Radio and Television
- On arrival of the Governor/Lieutenant Governor at formal State functions within his State/Union Territory and on his departure from such functions
- When the National Flag is brought on parade
Rules for mass singing
The National Song shall be played accompanied by mass singing on these occasions:
- On the unfurling of the National Flag, on cultural occasions or ceremonial functions other than parades
- On the arrival of the President at any Government or Public function (but excluding formal State functions) and also immediately before his departure from such functions
- On all occasions when the National Song is sung, the official version shall be recited accompanied by mass singing
- The National Song may be sung on occasions which, although not strictly ceremonial, are nevertheless invested with significance because of the presence of Ministers etc
- In all schools, the day’s work may begin with community singing of the National Song
Standing mandatory during National Song
The circular mentions specific rules of standing when the National Song is played or sung:
- Whenever the official version of the National Song is sung or played, the audience shall stand to attention.
- However, when, in the course of a newsreel or documentary, the National Song is played as part of the film, it is not expected of the audience to stand, as standing is bound to interrupt the exhibition of the film and would create disorder and confusion rather than add to the dignity of the National Song.
Vande Mataram: All six stanzas
The directive has given the lyrics for the National Song, and it includes all six stanzas of Vande Mataram. The lyrics to be sung or played are as follows:
Vande Mataram!
Sujalam suphalam malayaja-sitalam,
Sasya-syamalam Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Subhra-jyotsnam pulakita-yaminim,
Phulla-kusumita druma-dala-sobhinim,
Suhasinim sumadhura bhasinim,
Sukhadam varadam Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Koti-koti kantha kalakala ninada karale,
Koti-koti bhujair dhrta kharakaravale,
Ke bole Ma tumi abale!
Bahubaladharinim namami tarinim,
Ripudala-varinim Mataram!
Vande Mataram!
Tumi vidya, tumi dharma,
Tumi hrdi, tumi marma,
Tvam hi pranah sarire!
Bahute tumi Ma sakti,
Hrdaye tumi Ma bhakti,
Tomarai pratima gadi mandire-mandire.

A Karnataka Health Department Food Safety Division team resumed inspection of eateries and other establishments in Bengaluru on Wednesday (August 12, 2026).
The team inspected the canteen at the department’s headquarters in Bengaluru, where it seized expired food items and flagged hygiene violations.
Officials inspected hotels and other food business establishments located in the premises of Vidhana Soudha, Legislators’ Home and the MS Building in Bengaluru.
According to officials, expired food products, such as idli rava and coconut powder, were found in the kitchen of the Arogya Soudha canteen on Magadi Road. Food products were not stored in accordance with FSSAI guidelines. Pest control measures had not been carried out, leaving the premises in an unhygienic condition, officials said.
In a statement, the Food Safety and Drug Administration department said an advisory notice was issued in view of the unhygienic conditions observed at the canteen. Legal proceedings will be initiated before the Adjudicating Officer, it stated.
During inspection of a Nandini parlour located in the premises, officials found violations relating to labelling requirements, and issued an advisory notice, according to the statement.
Four hotels located in the premises of government buildings were inspected, with various deficiencies observed. Advisory notices were issued to the hotels concerned, according to the department.
Officials inspected a restaurant run by a private operator inside Legislators’ House, adjacent to Vidhana Soudha, and found unhygienic conditions. An advisory notice was issued. Among other things, cockroaches were found in the kitchen, they claimed.
A hotel located in the premises of the MS Building was inspected. The establishment was found to be unhygienic and was subsequently closed, the department stated.
The food business operator submitted an undertaking stating that the deficiencies would be rectified and that the hotel would be reopened only after obtaining permission from the Commissioner, in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the applicable rules, it stated.
Action would be initiated against the food business operator, the department added.
Eateries told to comply with food safety rules
Food business operators have been instructed to strictly comply with the Food Safety and Standards Act and the applicable rules and regulations, the department said.
Any violation relating to food quality, safety, hygiene, proper storage, labelling or food handling practices would invite strict legal action under the law, it added.
The department has been conducting such drives as part of special food safety inspections across all zones of Bengaluru Urban District and the Greater Bengaluru Area, covering three-star and five-star hotels to verify compliance with the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011.
Recently, 60 three-star and five-star hotels in Bengaluru Urban District were inspected, and 77 food samples were collected and sent to food laboratories for analysis.

The Assam Pradesh Congress Committee (APCC) on Wednesday (August 13, 2026) submitted a memorandum to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, urging him to declare the state's recurring flood and river erosion crisis a 'national problem'.
A delegation led by Pranjit Das, Chairman of the APCC Relief & Rehabilitation Department, met Assam Governor Lakshman Prasad Acharya and submitted the memorandum in this regard.
The flood situation in Assam improved on Wednesday (August 13, 2026) as the number of affected people dipped to 87,000 in four districts, but the toll climbed to 103 as two more deaths were reported.
In the memorandum, the Congress said around 40% of Assam's total land area, or 31.05 lakh hectares, is flood-prone, much higher than the national average of 10.2%.
It cited heavy siltation in the Brahmaputra and Barak basins, torrential monsoon rains, shallow riverbeds, embankment breaches and climate change impacts as key factors aggravating the situation.
The crisis has destroyed the livelihoods of farmers, daily wage labourers and tea garden workers, and displaced countless families, it added.
The APCC said the scale of the problem is beyond the capacity of the State government alone and demanded that the Centre recognise it as a "national problem" to ensure a permanent and scientific solution.
The party urged the Centre to set up a high-level task force comprising central and State officials, scientists, technical experts and representatives of affected people to find a solution to the perennial problem.
It also sought adequate central funds for a comprehensive master plan covering river course regulation, embankment strengthening, scientific dredging, real-time flood forecasting, early warning systems and planned rehabilitation of displaced families.
The memorandum further stressed the need for effective coordination among central ministries for integrated management of the Brahmaputra and its tributaries.
"Temporary relief alone cannot provide a lasting solution to this long-standing crisis," it added.

On the last day of the Parliament Monsoon Session on Thursday (August 13, 2026), Leader of the Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge in the Rajya Sabha condemned the ‘shuddhikaran’ (purification) ceremony reportedly held at Haldwani’s Ramlila Ground after he addressed a rally there on Saturday (August 8).
Uttarakhand Congress president Ganesh Godiyal alleged that the Shri Ram Sena, which conducted the ritual, had links to the BJP and the purification was done because Mr. Kharge is a Dalit. He accused the BJP of promoting caste-based divisions and described the incident as deeply objectionable.
“If Kharge ji is insulted, that means everyone is insulted,” said Rajya Sabha Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan before allowing Mr. Kharge to speak on the incident.
Parliament Monsoon Session Day 19 updates
“I say, with a lot if regret, that I went to deliver a public address at Haldwani. At that time, I did not take any religion’s name, only brought up people’s issues. After my speech, people of the BJP did a “shuddikaran”. Is this the way in democracy? How are you protecting the Constitution?” Mr. Kharge said, amid uproar.
Nadda says enquiry will be initiated
Leader of the House J.P. Nadda slammed the ‘shuddhikaran’ (purification) ceremony, saying that an enquiry will be initiated into the incident and action will be taken against the people involved. He also demanded a case to be registered under the Untouchability Act, saying, “Register a case against this act of untouchability. That is my demand,” Mr. Kharge said.

The Kerala High Court has claimed to have achieved a significant increase in the number of matters available for hearing and disposal through the recently introduced Auto Cause List System (ACLS) and the campaigns undertaken by the Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) to settle the cases.
The ACLS automatically identifies long-pending cases, prioritises them for listing before the appropriate Benches, and ensures regular and systematic listing of newly instituted cases. The campaign was led by Chief Justice Soumen Sen, according to a communication. Since its introduction on May 19, 2026, a total of 2,02,729 cases were listed before various Benches.
Of the 6,560 cases referred to the Kerala State Mediation and Conciliation Centre of the High Court from January to June 2026, as many as 724 cases were settled at the High Court and 18,110 cases in the district judiciary. The adalats conducted by the High Court Legal Services Committee and the National Lok Adalats organised across the State by the Kerala State Legal Services Authority (KeLSA) have settled 24,682 cases throughout the State. The High Court Legal Services Committee alone settled 70 cases in the High Court through the Adalats. The combined efforts of the agencies have helped the High Court achieve a higher case clearance ratio, according to a communication.
Victim compensation claims
KeLSA also facilitated the release of ₹48.23 crore for pending victim compensation claims across the State.
The scheme provides financial assistance to victims of crime, including women or their dependents, who have suffered loss or injury as a result of the crime and require rehabilitation, the communication said.

The Bihar cabinet on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) gave its nod to develop 300 ‘stand-alone’ private teacher education institutions (B.Ed.) operating in Bihar into multidisciplinary degree colleges.
The decision will add another 300 additional degree colleges which will offer undergraduate programmes in Arts, Science, Commerce, and other disciplines along with teacher education (B.Ed.) and skill-based courses, Cabinet Secretariat Department’s Secretary Mohammad Sohail said in a post cabinet briefing.
The decision was taken in accordance with the National Education Policy (NEP), 2020, and the guidelines of the National Council for Teacher Education (NCTE), he added.
The new academic programmes will be conducted in accordance with the standards and necessary approvals prescribed by the concerned university, UGC, NCTE, and the State government, Mr. Sohail said.
The initiative will provide students with greater opportunities for higher education within their own district or nearby areas, strengthen access to higher education, and contribute to increasing the state’s Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER), he added.
Extension of Schemes
It also gave the higher education department’s proposal to extend the Bihar Student Credit Card Scheme for another five years from 2026-27 to 2030-31, Mr. Sohail said, adding that ₹950 crore has been approved to be spent in the current financial year 2026-27.
Stating 4.15 lakh students have been benefitted from the SCC scheme, he said this decision will provide students in the State with greater opportunities for higher education, strengthen access to higher education, and promote an increase in the State’s Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER).
A step towards connecting Bihar’s youth with new age employment opportunities, the cabinet also extended the period of ‘Kushal Yuva Programme’ from 2026-27 to 2030-31 under ‘Seven Nischay Part-3’.
It approved ₹430.08 crore for imparting training to youth in future skills such as AI, drones, solar, networking, digital marketing, banking, telecom, foreign languages, and entrepreneurship, the Secretary said and added that it will directly create 6,436 employment opportunities and train 2,57,440 lakh youth annually.
Financial Assistance
In another decision, the cabinet also approved an estimated expenditure of ₹1,000 crore for a period of one year under “Pradhan Mantri Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana”, Mr. Sohail said, adding that the State government would give ₹10,000 per kilowatt subject to a maximum of ₹20,000 through DBT as financial assistance to the residential consumers for installing rooftop solar panels.
The State government’s financial assistance will be given in addition to the central government’s share, he added.
It also decided to set up Compressed Biogas (CBG) plants in four municipal corporations of Gaya Ji, Muzaffarpur, Bhagalpur and Biharsharif (Nalanda) for providing a sustainable solution for waste management by converting organic waste into a valuable renewable energy source, Mr. Sohail said.
The government would give 10 acres of land for a period of 25 years to IOCL, HPCL, BPCL and GAIL for the purpose, he said adding that CBG plants process organic waste and convert it into a valuable energy resource, thereby improving waste management.
Restriction lifted
In yet another decision, the cabinet also lifted the restriction imposed on the purchase, sale, and transfer of land in the notified Greenfield Satellite Cities following the final publication of the Development Plan, Mr. Sohail said.
In addition, the Bihar Urban Development Authority will have the power to lift the restriction on the purchase, sale, and transfer of land after the publication of the draft Development Plan.
The cabinet also approved the Youth, Employment and Skill Development Department’s proposal to amend the admission process for the State’s Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) and to conduct admissions to 50% of the total sanctioned seats in private Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs through the Bihar Combined Entrance Competitive Examination Board (BCECEB), Patna.
A total of 11 decisions were taken at cabinet meeting chaired by Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary on Wednesday (August 12, 2026).

At the pre-release event of the Telugu film Agadha in Hyderabad, Dr Kamakshi Bhaskarla became emotional as she spoke about playing the central character in a film for the first time. It had taken her nine years to reach this point, she said, thanking the audience for their support. Directed by MS Raju, the thriller releases in theatres on August 14.
Settling down for this interview, Kamakshi says she is still a work in progress. “I had to make tough choices in life. There were times when I wanted to give up. But I used the opportunities that came my way to build my career; I had no godfather in the industry.”
Kamakshi made her Telugu cinema debut with Priyuralu and went on to act in several web series and films, including the recent Dacoit. The horror-thriller Maa Oori Polimera proved to be a turning point. She is now working on Polimera 3 and the second season of the web series Dhootha. In her early years, she says, she chose some films for visibility and financial independence, while also gravitating towards characters that represented everyday women.
“In Agadha, my character Mahadevi is central to the film, and it has taken me a while to reach this space,” she says. Kamakshi is aware that her roles in the Polimera franchise, Virupaksha and now Agadha may lead audiences to associate her with thrillers. “Love stories and thrillers remain the most common genres in Telugu cinema where women get to shine. It would be lovely to see well-written comedies that give female characters ample scope.”
Aspiring to write and direct
She dreams of writing and directing a feature film and is pursuing an online screenwriting course. “I worked as an assistant director on Polimera and hope to direct someday. I enjoy work that stimulates me emotionally and intellectually.”
That search for creative and intellectually challenging work led her to theatre before cinema. After returning from China in 2017 with a medical degree, she briefly explored modelling before joining theatre groups Samahaara in Hyderabad and Neeraj Kabi’s group in Mumbai. “Modelling did not interest me. Theatre gave me the creative freedom I was looking for.”
The shift from medicine to theatre and cinema was a conscious attempt to carve out her own path. “I grew up in a middle-class family, in dysfunctional circumstances. I admired the strength of the women in my family but also saw how their voices were suppressed.” She says moving to China for medical studies was partly an attempt to break free and grow independently.
In her early years, she approached production houses and auditioned extensively. “Word got around that there’s a doctor-turned-actor who is good at auditions and is a promising actor,” she recalls with a smile.
She gravitated towards characters representing women often overlooked by mainstream cinema. She played a househelp in Priyuralu and a woman from the fishing community in Polimera. “Such characters are often relegated to supporting parts or not celebrated like the archetypal heroine roles,” she says.
Behavioural psychology
Her understanding of human psychology, she says, helps her inhabit these characters with confidence. “It was one of the subjects in medical school; it taught me to read between the lines and understand a character better.”
While Kamakshi enjoys hearing directors narrate a story, she reads each script several times. “I might have read the script of Polimera over 20 times. I read between the lines to understand what the writer or director intends to convey and whether that intent comes through. If something doesn’t add up, I discuss it with them. Most directors have been welcoming of these conversations.”
Reading has been a source of comfort since childhood. “That was my safe space. I enjoyed having imaginary conversations with the characters in a story.” She is currently reading The Palace of Illusions, a habit that has also sharpened her ability to assess scripts.
Away from film sets, Kamakshi enjoys solo travel and trekking, and hopes to climb Mt Kilimanjaro. “Wherever I travel, I choose homestays so I can be around people and observe them.”
Among women in Telugu cinema, she admires Samantha Ruth Prabhu for shaping her career and building the stardom to headline female-centric films. She also admires Nithya Menen and Nivetha Thomas. “There are a hundred ways to work and survive, but I am consciously choosing films that excite me. I hope my work is emotionally satisfying too.”

The Supreme Court of India on Thursday (August 13, 2026) asked the union government to consider a petition filed by an apex court lawyer flagging the lack of a comprehensive statutory regime on the government’s use of “high-risk” Artificial Intelligence technology in areas affecting public access to food, health benefits, wages, pension, scholarship and grant of welfare subsidies.
A three-judge Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant asked the government to consider the detailed petition of advocate N.K. Goswami as a representation for taking comprehensive action.
In his petition, Mr. Goswami questioned whether the government could employ AI, machine learning (ML), automated decision-making systems, risk-scoring mechanisms, biometric surveillance tools, predictive policing technologies and AI-assisted content moderation systems in crucial areas of governance affecting welfare, liberty, privacy, dignity, livelihood and speech, without a “specific statutory framework” or meaningful human oversight.
The lawyer clarified that the constitutional vice pleaded in the petition was not that technology must be prohibited.
“The vice is that technology affecting fundamental rights cannot be permitted to operate outside the discipline of the Constitution. When a citizen’s access to food, health benefits, wages, pension, scholarship, subsidy, liberty, privacy or speech is affected by an opaque automated or semi-automated system, the State must satisfy the minimum constitutional requirements,” Mr. Goswami submitted.
The petition said he was only trying to constitutionalise innovation.
“AI is no longer merely an administrative aid or technological convenience. It has begun to enter the bloodstream of governance. Public-domain official materials, policy and supporting documents show that AI/ML, automated decision-making, fraud-detection, beneficiary-verification, Aadhaar-linked authentication, data-driven de-duplication and similar algorithmic systems are being used in welfare-linked governance, from health-benefit delivery to ration-distribution optimisation to fraud-prevention,” it said.
The Chief Justice said the petition raised technical issues in the policy domain, and the court lacked the necessary technical know-how to address them.
Mr Goswami argued that the court could indeed intervene to fill the legislative gap, given the lack of any statutory mechanism governing the use of AI/ML in public welfare.
The petition had sought that the court direct the Centre to file a “complete affidavit” disclosing all existing and proposed high-risk AI systems used by Union Ministries/agencies in welfare, policing, surveillance and content regulation, together with their legal basis, vendor/agency, purpose, data categories, safeguards, grievance mechanism and audit status.

In 1989 when Collin Timms opened a Mexican restaurant in Bengaluru named after a river in New Mexico, Pecos, it bombed. People were simply not familiar with the cuisine. It is another story that Pecos eventually pivoted to selling beer and became the city’s favourite pub. Today, things are very different when it comes to Mexican food. Carne asadas and birria tacos are fast selling dishes in the city’s new age restaurants, that focus on regional dishes and authenticity. We trace this evolution and explore the new fascination Bengaluru has for the cuisine.
Chef Varun Pereira, the man behind the restaurant Comal, says, “There has been a huge increase in interest for Mexican cuisine. Even the Tex Mex places are now adding Mexican dishes to their menus. I feel it is a very unexplored cuisine. Mexican was never as popular as Italian or Asian. But there is a huge connect between Indian and Mexico.” At Comal you can dine on masa flour tortillas and chilaquiles. The focus is on using techniques, tools (comal means tawa) and ingredients. The tortillas are made with nixtamalization of corn flour and the enchiladas have mole sauce. Their best sellers are jackfruit flautas (rolled-up tacos), horchata, the rice-based drink, and carne asadas (grilled and sliced meat dish).
Varun, with co-founder Pratheek Reddy travelled to Mexico City for a month and ate in Michelin-starred restaurants and street tacos. “I am a big fan of Mexican cuisine, and there was always a gap in the market, and I wanted to bring my love for this food to India and Bengaluru.”
At Comal there are tables facing the open kitchen so guests can chat and give immediate feedback to the chefs. He says the Bengaluru diner is open to new cuisines, compared to other cities. “We get guests who are not familiar with the cuisine and want to be guided through, it is nice to have that option.”
Cantina culture
For restauranteur Rizwan Amlani, opening Mezcalita, a cantina-style establishment was a labour of love. When he was in his 20s, working as a chef in the US, he would go to Mexico often and it almost felt like home. His passion for the country and knowledge of the cuisine is evident as he describes to me the difference between a cantina, a taquería, and a fondita (it is a home-style eatery, if you are curious).
“A cantina is a friendly casual establishment. The bartends will know your name, it is a family affair. It is like an Irani cafe in Mumbai. I go to the same Irani cafe, my great grandfather went to.” Mezcalita has outlets in Mumbai and Bengaluru, and their top sellers are the Baja fish taco, pork carnitas and green enchiladas. The Bengaluru diner, he says, is the most experimental and curious. “My team is challenged every day because people ask a lot of questions. They want to know how it is cooked, what are the spices, why is it so familiar. This is rarer in Mumbai.”
Chocolate in my gravy?
Chinita is a one of the few Mexican restaurants that opened a decade ago. “When we first started, we spent a lot of time on the floor talking to customers, educating them about the cuisine and explaining the various dishes on our menu. Over the last 12 years, we’ve noticed that the cuisine has become more widely accepted and popular, and customers are more knowledgeable about Mexican food now,” says Sameer Mirchandani, the managing partner at the restaurant that has outlets in Koramangala and Indiranagar.
“I remember certain traditional Mexican combinations used to generate a lot of interest, such as chocolate and chilli in our chocolate chilli cake, and the idea of using chocolate in a main course like in our mole.” Their soft tacos, burrito bowls, chocolate chilli cake, and Mexican-style grilled corn have been some of the best-sellers from the start.
Another restaurant in Indiranagar serving regional Mexican food is the newly opened Comedor. With a vegetarian only menu, it has dishes such as chile relleno (stuffed chillies) that hail from the city of Puebla, and Sopa de fideo (a vermicelli soup with Spanish roots). Ingredients such as Mexican pepperleaf, masa flour, cojita cheese and the root vegetable jicama are used in the dishes.
Rizwan feels there are not enough Mexican spaces in India. “Bengaluru diners are experimental, but I feel like every market in India is still not ready to go down that path yet. However, there is scope in the future for regional Mexican food.” He compares it to how Asian food used to be monolith earlier, and now we have specialty spaces. “I would love to do an Oxacan restaurant someday.”

Rohini Rana’s new cookbook Memories on a Platter: My Fusion Cookbook begins with a dedication to the three women who ignited a love of cooking in her – her mother, her sister-in-law and her husband’s nanny — a flame that, decades later, continues to burn.
Born into royalty to Raja Digvijay Pal Singh and Rani Anant Kumari of Awagarh in Uttar Pradesh, Rohini married Gaurav Shumsher Jung Bahadur Rana, who went on to become the Chief of Army Staff, Nepal Army, from 2012 to 2015.
“During the eight months between my engagement and marriage, my mother realised that I had not learnt any cooking skills – owing to my years of staying in hostel dorms and only coming home for the holidays. So, my sister-in-law, Rani Saheba Anjali Kumari, was tasked with teaching me how to cook. From making eggs-to-order to sandwiches and cakes as well as Indian dishes, she taught me all, and I absorbed it like a sponge!”, Rohini recalls with a smile. As a newly-married bride in Nepal, it was her husband’s childhood nanny, Chiniya Champa didi, who taught her cooking. “I’ve been a foodie my whole life. I guess that is what led to my interest in cooking because once you’re fond of eating good food, you want to know how to make it,” she says.
It was out of sheer boredom, when her husband was posted somewhere in the hills, and she found herself the sole woman among a battalion of 800 men, that she decided to pen down an introduction to her first book — The Rana Cookbook: Recipes from the Palaces of Nepal. “I realised that my husband’s nanny was getting old and soon, all that knowledge about Nepalese heritage cuisine would be lost,” she says. The Nepal Cookbook: 108 Regional Recipes followed soon after, both books earning recognition for preserving Nepal’s culinary heritage.
Her third book, Memories on a Platter: My Fusion Cookbook, published by Penguin Random House, was launched recently in the presence of Jyotiraditya M Scindia, Union Minister of Communications. The collection draws inspiration from Rohini’s childhood in India, her years within Nepal’s illustrious Rana family after her marriage, and the diverse cuisines she encountered while accompanying her husband on diplomatic and military assignments around the world. “Having exhausted my Nepali repertoire, I was thinking about what to do next. I think the more you grow older, the more you drift back to your childhood memories. So, I have a lot of Indian recipes in this book, but since it is fusion, there is Nepali cuisine as well as cuisines from places such as Italy, Japan, China, Kenya, Lebanon, Cambodia, the United Kingdom, and Malaysia among many others,” she shares.
Divided into sections such as global bites, centrestage, vibrant crunchy bowls, sweet traditions and liquid delights, the book blends anecdotes from her life with inventive cross-cultural dishes. A great love for all things chaat (she is from UP, after all!) led to a recipe with golgappas, but since this is also fusion, she suggests fillings such as scrambled eggs and salmon, or corn and edamame. Elsewhere, mini makki ki rotis meet melted brie, and buckwheat crepes take on ham and cheese.
“Most of these dishes came out of experiments, and I have, hopefully, taken them to a different level. In a way, this book is my memoir told through food,” she smiles, revealing that she does have an idea for her next cookbook — inspired by India, again — but for now, she is simply enjoying sharing these delicious chapters of her life. As she writes in the introduction — “This book is not in the pursuit of perfection but in the pursuit of joy, the pleasure I gain from being creative and feeding people, which to me is a language of love…”
