The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government in Kerala on Thursday (August 13, 2026) edged closer to ordering a multi-angled investigation into the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) government’s “bungled attempt” to bring the 2021 FIFA World Cup-winning Argentina team and its iconic captain, Lionel Messi, for a friendly match at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Kochi in 2025.
Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan told a press conference that the State Sports Department’s preliminary inquiry into the alleged fiasco, which left football fans profoundly disappointed, revealed “very serious allegations” warranting further investigation by multiple departments and agencies.
(The charges in the report, vetted by Sports Department Special Secretary N. Prasanth, reportedly included massive service tax fraud on foreign remittances, contraventions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), abuse of power resulting in loss to the public exchequer, and “shady financial transactions” involving offshore entities, among other charges.)
Mr Satheesan said the previous government “cannot not shrug off responsibility” centred around the controversy by airing “contradictory statements”.
He said several questions remain unanswered. “What was the procedure followed by the previous government to permit the private sponsor (a television news broadcasting company) to transact with the Argentine Football Association (AFA) on behalf of the State without inviting an expression of intent, a legal pre-requisite before entering into a final binding contract or agreement? Did the government examine the source of the private sponsor’s funding? Did it conduct a market price determination before contemplating a binding legal contract or agreement with the private sponsor?”, Mr Satheesan asked.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her role later this month, depriving U.S. President Donald Trump of his chief spokesperson less than three months before the November midterm elections. Ms. Leavitt has served as the press secretary since Mr. Trump returned to office in 2025.
Karoline Leavitt to step down
Mr. Trump announced the move on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) in a post on social media. He said Ms. Leavitt was stepping down to spend more time with her family and would “now be one of my top outside advisors”. She recently gave birth to her second child.
In a separate post, Ms. Leavitt said she was “incredibly grateful” for the opportunity to serve, but added that the position had placed significant demands on her family. She said Mr. Trump had asked her to continue as a “top advisor to him on the outside”.
“The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of the White House Press Secretary,” she wrote.
Mr. Trump said Ms. Leavitt “will be departing her role at the end of the month so she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family, a decision I totally understand and respect! Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party, as we work to defy History, and conclusively win the Midterm Elections.”
The President did not immediately name a successor, and the White House did not respond to questions about who would replace her.
Trump’s ‘trusted aide’
Mr. Trump, then President-elect, announced on November 15, 2024, that Ms. Leavitt would serve as White House press secretary.
Ms. Leavitt succeeded Karine Jean-Pierre on January 20, 2025, when Mr. Trump was sworn in as the 47th President of the United States. She had previously served as the Trump campaign’s national press secretary and worked in the first Trump administration as the assistant press secretary. While announcing her appointment, the President had said that she was smart, tough, and a highly effective communicator
Ms. Leavitt has been among the most prominent advocates of Mr. Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) campaign. Mr. Trump described her as “one of my most trusted aides”.
Youngest White House press secretary
Ms. Leavitt, 28, became the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary when she assumed office last year. She previously worked as a junior spokesperson during Mr. Trump’s first term and later became a leading spokeswoman for his 2024 presidential campaign after an unsuccessful congressional bid in New Hampshire in 2022.
She recently returned to work following maternity leave after the birth of her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a two-year-old son.
During Ms. Leavitt’s maternity leave in May, the White House held fewer press briefings and did not appoint an interim spokesperson. Instead, senior officials, including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, conducted media briefings.
Combative approach towards media
During her tenure at the White House, Ms. Leavitt became known for her combative exchanges with the media and her staunch defence of the President.
During Mr. Trump’s first term, Ms. Leavitt served as a press aide in the White House press office before becoming the communications director to New York Republican Representative Elise Stefanik.
In his second term, with Ms. Leavitt as a key public advocate, the White House adopted an even more confrontational media strategy than during his first administration. While Mr. Trump frequently engaged directly with reporters at White House events and during official travel, Ms. Leavitt often appeared on Fox News and other conservative outlets to promote the administration’s agenda and criticise Democrats and mainstream media organisations.
Ms. Leavitt’s departure comes at a challenging time for the U.S. President, who is facing difficulties in finding a path forward on the conflict involving Iran, while also confronting concerns over the economy. These issues have weighed on the President’s approval ratings and raised concerns among Republicans about retaining control of Congress in the midterm elections.

The YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) has urged the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), Andhra Pradesh, and the Election Commission of India (ECI) to make the verification process for electors whose records have been classified as unmapped or mismatched more voter-friendly.
In a representation to the CEO on Wednesday (August 12, 2026), YSRCP State general secretary and MLC Lella Appi Reddy sought uniform instructions across the State on three issues: allowing parents or blood relatives to submit documents on behalf of electors, making the verification venue mandatory in every notice, and providing assistance through Booth Level Officers (BLOs). The party released the letter to the media on Thursday.
Mr. Appi Reddy said in the representation that many affected electors could be students, employees, migrant workers or persons temporarily residing away from their native places, and might not be able to appear personally on the date specified in the notice. He requested that parents or blood relatives be permitted to submit the required documents on behalf of such electors, along with proof of relationship and proper authorisation. This, he said, would help ensure that genuine voters were not excluded merely because they could not be physically present.
Mr. Appi Reddy also said that in some notices, the place of verification had reportedly been left blank. A voter could not reasonably be expected to comply with a notice without knowing where to appear, he said.
He urged the authorities to ensure that every notice clearly mentioned the exact venue, date, time and details of the officer concerned before it was served on the elector.
He also called for greater involvement of BLOs in the verification process. Instead of requiring every elector to approach a higher-level electoral officer personally, the BLO concerned should be involved in receiving documents and conducting preliminary or field-level verification, he suggested.
The final statutory decision could continue to rest with the competent Electoral Registration Officer or Assistant Electoral Registration Officer, while BLO-level facilitation would enable voters to resolve discrepancies locally and quickly, he said.
Mr. Appi Reddy appealed to the Election Commission to issue uniform State-wide instructions on the three issues so that no genuine elector was excluded merely because of procedural difficulties, temporary absence from the constituency or lack of clarity in the verification notice.

The Lok Sabha recently passed an amendment to a law to make it legal to levy surcharges or fees on any UPI and RuPay debit card transactions. The government, meanwhile, announced that it proposes to do so only for purchases of ₹2,000 and more from businesses with a threshold of turnover. But with the legal bar removed, government decisions can change any time.
The stated logic, as the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor Sanjay Malhotra recently put it, is that “somebody has to pay” for UPI. The Indian government is said to have subsidised UPI by about ₹2,000 crore in the past one year.
Let us first examine the stated reason, and then come to what most knowledgeable people think is the real reason.
Digital payments such as UPI and debit cards replace the centuries-old payment system of bank notes and coins. The latter can be called physical currency as against the new digital currency. Who paid for the bank notes payment system? The RBI printed notes and minted coins and gave them to the banks for no charges. One can walk into a bank and demand currency notes for all the deposits one held, and they would have to be made available free of charge, even in the precise denominations asked for, subject to availability (though the printing and logistic costs of small notes for the same amount is much more than of big notes).
So, if the government — through the RBI — funded the earlier/ traditional payments system, or more widely, the cost of the “operating medium” of economic exchanges, what prevents it from doing it now as well. What has changed? In fact, a digital “payments system” is far less costly, and much more efficient, than a physical currency-based one.
What is a digital payment system? A user is at a shop and wants to make a purchase. She gives a secure message to her bank to withdraw and spend her own money. Instead of the bank handing them the needed cash, and user giving it to the merchant, and the merchant then depositing it in his bank — a tedious, and quite costly process — a set of instant secure messages just ensures that the user’s account is debited and the merchant’s, perhaps in another bank, credited the same amount. Why should this relatively trivial and inexpensive process — replacing a much more cumbersome and costlier one — be required to separately be paid for, when cash movement itself was not paid for?
If the government spent ₹2,000 crore on UPI last year, it also saved nearly ₹1,500 crore over the same time in reduced expenditure on printing currency notes. This saving is going to go up fast, as digital means replace currency, while UPI operating costs could remain similar, or actually come down as technology advances. If digital systems incur costs on security, physical cash systems also require them, even if of a different kind.
Public goods are generally free
But why should the government make such expenditures at all without recouping them, if possible? There is a very sound economic logic for it. Less or near-nil friction in the payments system, through zero costing of transactions, considerably increases economic flows. The overall economy benefits multiple times more than any possible collection of transaction surcharges. This is the typical public goods logic. This is why governments erect lighthouses on the shores and develop parks in cities. Charging users for such services tend to reduce or distort their use and benefits to such an extent that it is judged unfavourably.
First-time visitors to some European cities are pleasantly surprised when their hotel gives them a transport pass for their entire stay, which is provided free by the city. Such a free pass greatly increases the mobility of the tourists through the city, rather than them scouring for change for every small ride. Tourists moving around spend more money, and do it across the city. The overall economy of the city benefits a lot. Even the government is likely to get back more in sales taxes from such extra spending than what they lost in providing free transport passes.
Similarly, the way increased mobility can increase economic activity — which is why many countries have traditionally subsidised motor fuel — reduced friction in economic transactions does it even more. That is why bank notes were never charged for their production and logistic costs. There is no reason that governments and central banks should charge for the less costly and much more efficient (economic activity expanding) digital payment system. As said, that is just sound economic logic.
If banknote payments require no surcharges or fees, why should digital payments incur them, in a digital world? After all, digital payments means less work and less costs of all kinds for almost everyone involved. When the public goods argument works for physical currency, why should it fail for digital currency?
The real reason
Let us now move to the real reasons for what is happening. Many countries such as Brazil, Indonesia, Vietnam, Turkey, and so on, now have a UPI-like system. Both India and Brazil have repeatedly been named in U.S. official documents regarding their digital payment systems being “unfair trade practices”. In July 2026, the U.S. government imposed a 25% tariff on a range of imports from Brazil, explicitly citing Brazil’s free, state-run instant payment system, Pix, as an unfair trade barrier that disadvantages American financial companies such as Visa and Mastercard.
The India-U.S. trade deal is nearly ready, though its details remain secret. India is currently checking the boxes on U.S. demands. It can be said with almost complete certainty that India has bent where Brazil stood firm. This is why it amended the law which disallowed surcharges on UPI. So that Visa and MasterCard do not suffer. One already sees at retail stores and petrol pumps, merchants making excuses that their credit card machine is not working, and preferring UPI payments, which saves them a considerable surcharge. U.S. President Donald Trump could not let top U.S. financial corporations lose major markets.
When U.S. credit companies emerged, it was a digital innovation over a mainstream physical currency system. Making instant secure communication for payments was quite expensive. Today, it is a rather trivial technology, and the system is much cheaper than physical currency. Also, digital is mainstream today. Some banks worldwide charge for physical interactions, while providing the digital ones free. India suddenly now bringing in fees for digital payments is going against both the economic and technological logic.
Let UPI remain a public good
One thing the Indian government has boasted about the most in the last many years, nationally and internationally, is India’s UPI. It is shocking that under U.S.’s pressure India is willing to change the basic logic and architecture of its most vaunted achievement. Just so that the business model of Visa and Mastercard is not affected. This does not speak well about Indian sovereignty. If Brazil could stand firm, why cannot India?
By banning surcharges or fees on UPI, India will continue to reap the immense gains in terms of economic ease, efficiency and expansion that come from it. UPI is today also a matter of inclusion and social justice. We need not import the U.S. model which wants to see everything, even payment systems, as a market good. UPI should stay a public good, and free.
India should promote a competitive field of payment players, preferably domestic, and leverage a public and free switch of UPI. That way, VIsa and Mastercard, and other foreign companies, may not rule over one of the biggest assets of Indian payments data.
Parminder Jeet Singh is a Delhi-based digital society researcher and activist

Variety is literally the spice of life in Andhra cuisine.
The region is traditionally known as the ‘spice heartland of India’, and there is no getting away from the range of fiery masalas - like Guntur Sannam chillies, gongura leaves, turmeric, ginger, and mustard seeds - that add so much ‘oomph’ to Andhra dishes. Chennai has always played host to a large Telugu community from different walks of life, making Andhra cuisine immensely popular in the city for its distinctive spices and traditional recipes. Their hospitality comes alive at some of the city’s iconic eateries. Here is our pick.
The National Lodge
Third-generation family member Satyanarayana Deepak says, “When my grandfather, K Ethiraj established the National Lodge in 1952, it functioned as a lodging house and a restaurant. Businessmen from across the Madras Presidency would come to Sowcarpet for trade. For many, especially those from Andhra, this became the preferred place to stay and enjoy homely Andhra food.” Today, Deepak, along with his brother, Satyanarayana Dwarak and son, Vidhant, manage the Sowcarpet and Mount Road outlets, serving nearly 120 diners at a time.
As with most traditional Andhra cuisine, the meals are the highlight of the day. Once the rice is served, the National special parupu podi arrives, and either raw tamarind chutney, gongura pachadi or tomato thokku are served in turns. The piece-de-resistance arrives with the second serving of rice — a delicious bowl of vada sambar. The leaf is further adorned with poriyal, pickle, pachadi, rasam, buttermilk and finally, curd with sugar! It is evidently, the quality that has sustained them for as long.
Sowcarpet and Anna Salai, Phone: 9840161919.
New Andhra Meals Hotel
Towards the eastern end of Pondy Bazaar, Chennai’s shopping hub, stands the New Andhra Meals Hotel, drawing a steady stream of patrons as well as first time diners who arrive on recommendation.
“We serve the traditional vegetarian meals on the banana leaf, with the option of non-vegetarian side dishes. If requested we also serve non-vegetarian gravies,” says P Balakrishna, the owner, who is known to be at the outlets early each day. The Pondy Bazaar branch has been managed by Venkatesan since 2001, while Balakrishna’s close associate Prakash oversees operations here as well as at the newer Valasaravakkam outlet.
The highlight of their Andhra meals is the generously sized vanjaram fry, along with succulent Andhra prawns, with the fish sourced from a regular vendor in Zam Bazaar. With these two items on the leaf, everything else takes a back seat, though the rest of the fare holds its own. The Nellore rice which is specially sourced, compliments dishes such as karakozhambu, sambar, rasam and morekolambu. “Guntur chicken, Hyderabad chicken 65, mutton and gongura are prepared by using our own spices,” says Balakrishna, adding that their mutton, chicken and egg biryanis are equally popular.
I am told that very little has changed in their menu over the years. “It has always been selectively curated and only the most sought-after dishes are featured,” says Balakrishna. “However, due to popular demand we have introduced tandoori chicken, chapathi and parotta.”
T Nagar, Phone: 7708099915.
Amaravathi, Cathedral Road
At Amaravathi, the second generation, represented by Nivruti Reddy, is a constant presence at the flagship outlet on Cathedral Road, even as she manages her time across other establishments. When I walk into Amaravathi at lunch time, the place is packed. “The sourcing of raw materials and preparation are carefully coordinated, a process refined over the years. Every ingredient is made in-house,” she says, joining me at the table.
Amaravathi is best known for its meals, popular both during lunch and dinner. “Our in-house preparations like rotu pachchadi and ragi ball with Andhra fish pulusu are in constant demand,” says Ramesh, the manager. As the banana leaf is filled with chutneys, pickles, and thokkus, the ragi ball catches my eye. Dipped in the spicy fish curry, it tastes divine.
I wonder if the health conscious diner still indulges in Andhra cuisine. Alongside the traditional vegetarian meals, complimented by non-vegetarian side dishes, the biryani platter is a popular choice. It features four small portions each of mutton, chicken, and prawn biryani along with white rice. Diners can also opt for three non-vegetarain gravies as add-ons. Not to be missed are the highlights — Andhra chicken and vanjaram fry. The meal ends with a delicious tumbler of South Indian coffee. A fitting end.
Mylapore. Phone: 9500020011.
Velidis, Ramapuram
After several years as an advertising professional, V Veeraiah chose to follow a passion and enter the food industry, taking on the responsibility of managing the kitchen of a leading club in the city. “That the speciality of the club was Andhra cuisine was coincidental, given my family background as chilli growers from Chirala,” says Veeraiah.
When an opportunity arose, he decided toopen Velidis (named after his family) in the busy Ramapuram locality in 2004. “That’s when I realised that the area was already crowded with many Andhra messes serving meals for much below ₹100 a plate,” recalls Veeraiah. Undeterred, he curated a distinctive menu of Andhra dishes. Velidis special chicken biryani and Velidis joint chicken biryani, both topped with Megana chicken dry or Aalfa chicken dry are the most popular dishes. “That we source the best quality Guntur chillies and use only basmati rice for our biryanis, has ensured the top quality in taste. For our seafood dishes, fresh vanjaram and prawns are procured daily and we do not refrigerate them for the next day,” informs Veeraiah.
The biryani has a distinct flavour and I am told the dishes are cooked on coal, as are their tandoori preparations. The success of Velidis at Ramapuram has encouraged him to open another outlet in Pallavaram.
Manapakkam. Phone: 9380938513.

Congress MP Renuka Chowdhury has written to Chief Minister Revanth Reddy of the Congress-led government in Telangana, asking that the State government take a position in the Supreme Court to support the Constitutional challenges to the recently passed amendments to the Transgender Rights law that removed the right to self-identification of gender identity.
The law, passed in Parliament this March, ran into widespread protests from the transgender community across the country and had also led to resignations from members appointed to the Government’s National Council for Transgender Persons over provisions that mandate medical certification of gender identity instead of relying on self-identification.
Ms. Chowdhury, whose opposition to the amendments has been vocal, inside and outside Parliament, has now asked the Congress government in Telangana to support the challenges to the amendment that are currently being heard in the Supreme Court of India. In a letter to Mr. Reddy, the Congress’ Rajya Sabha MP from Telangana said, “I would earnestly request the Government of Telangana to extend its support to these proceedings through the office of the Learned Additional Advocate General, Shri Rajnikanth Reddy, by assisting the court in defence of the constitutional rights and dignity of transgender persons.”
In addition to this, Ms. Chowdhury has also requested the Telangana government to “carefully examine the administrative, financial and implementation implications of the new Act” for the State. She noted that this was needed to look at where the amended Act “may conflict with the State’s existing welfare architecture and its commitment to protecting the rights of transgender persons”.
Ms. Chowdhury noted in her letter to the Telangana CM that the State has “consistently stood for inclusion, social justice, and constitutional morality, and its intervention at this stage would carry both legal and moral significance.”
She also noted that during the debate on the amendments in Rajya Sabha, the Congress party had strongly opposed the legislation on the grounds that it undermined the principles of dignity, equality, and self-identification recognised by the Supreme Court, and “strikes at the heart of the guarantees under Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21 of our Constitution”.
At the time the Bill was being introduced and discussed, a delegation of trans activists from across the country had also met with the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi and Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra in New Delhi, following which the official account of the Indian National Congress had posted a statement saying that Mr. Gandhi reiterated that the “Congress party stands firmly with the rights and dignity of transgender persons and will oppose the Bill in Parliament”.
Soon after the amendments to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act were passed, several challenges to it were filed before the Supreme Court of India, which has issued notice in these matters to the Union government. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for August 17.

Andhra:2018 Andhra Group-I exam riddled with irregularities, say SIT probe
Amaravati, An SIT probing the 2018 Andhra Pradesh Group-I recruitment examination has uncovered alleged irregularities across multiple stages of evaluation, including the use of unauthorised evaluators, purported manual evaluation at a private resort and widespread alterations in OMR evaluation sheets.
The probe pertains to Andhra Pradesh Public Service Commission's recruitment of 169 Group- I posts through a notification issued in 2018. It attracted more than 1.14 lakh applications.
"An SIT probing the 2018 Andhra Pradesh Group-I recruitment examination, the state's premier civil services examination has uncovered serious irregularities across multiple stages," said a press release.
The SIT was constituted by the Andhra Pradesh government in February 2026, following directions from the High Court to scientifically examine allegations of tampering and irregularities in the recruitment process.
According to the SIT, alleged irregularities had occurred during three separate evaluation exercises - the original digital valuation in 2021, a purported manual valuation conducted at a private resort following a High Court order, and a second manual valuation conducted at Vijayawada in 2022 during the erstwhile YSRCP government.
During the digital evaluation, the SIT alleged that unauthorised evaluators, private e-mail and mark discrepancies had occurred, adding that the first major irregularities arose during digital evaluation of the mains stage of the examination.
"The SIT found that the decision to introduce digital evaluation, as well as the panel of evaluators engaged for the exercise did not carry the mandatory approval of the PSC Chairman," said the press release.
Out of a secretary-approved panel of 158 evaluators, only 72 actually evaluated the answer scripts while another 25 persons who were not on the approved panel also evaluated answer scripts and were paid, the SIT claimed.
The approved panel itself predominantly consisted of teachers and lecturers from private schools and colleges instead of the university-level subject experts contemplated by the PSC Office Manual, it said.
The digital evaluation was coordinated through an unofficial private e-mail account, personal email accounts and Google Drive links, said the SIT.
The probe noted alleged differences between marks originally entered by the evaluators and the marks reflected in the final digital-result database.
The SIT noted that the second-evaluation marks were allegedly entered in several cases without an independent second examiner, with one freelancer, Mahamkali Raghuram, making such entries himself.
The SIT observed that the PSC paid ₹1.38 crore to Stone Media Advisory Services and TrueGrader for the digital evaluation exercise, adding that Raghuram received approximately ₹10 lakh towards evaluation and coordination work.
Following candidates challenging the digital evaluation in the High Court, it ordered a manual evaluation, observing that the notified methodology to digital valuation was contrary to the recruitment notification.
Later, the SIT noted that manual evaluation was undertaken at a private resort, which was not a government office but a private space, where "manual evaluation" amounted to only allegedly re-entering the earlier digital marks.
According to the SIT, answer scripts had remained in a private agency's custody for 84 days and accused the then PSC secretary PSR Anjaneyulu over the manual evaluation irregularities.
Further, it noted that the second manual evaluation was conducted in Vijayawada after D Gautam Sawang took charge of the PSC in February 2022.
However, the SIT alleged that there was no documentary record supporting the policy decision of the then PSC chairman, Sawang, to conduct the second manual evaluation.
In the second manual evaluation, the SIT claimed that there were several discrepancies, such as alleged 95 percent alterations or over-writings, different inks and handwritings and others.
Highlighting that forensic material was examined by Central Forensic Science Laboratory in Hyderabad, New Delhi, Shimla, Pune, Bhopal, Kolkata and Guwahati, the SIT raised concerns over the custody and surveillance of confidential examination material.
It found that there was allegedly no CCTV coverage over the PSC Confidential Sections or the Strong Room during the original examination period.
"During the fresh manual valuation in 2022, cameras were initially installed only in two confidential-section rooms. The Strong Room itself came under CCTV only on April 11, 2022 17 days after valuation began," said the press release.
Even after cameras were installed, the SIT found multiple alleged inconsistencies between CCTV footage and the official Guard Register.
The SIT additionally found that most examiners were allegedly using mobile phones inside the manual evaluation camps and another inconsistency was the unusually large number of answer scripts that required a third evaluation.
According to PSC, only 0.45 percent of scripts required third evaluation in the previous Group-I recruitment, compared with alleged 10.2 percent in the 2018 recruitment process.
"The SIT said that while this alone could not establish wrongdoing, the dramatic increase, taken together with over-writing, unauthenticated corrections, signature mismatches and other forensic irregularities, indicated serious inconsistency in the evaluation process," the release said.
A criminal case was registered in April 2025 under Sections 409, 477-A, 420 and 120-B read with Section 34 of the IPC.
Camsign Media Director P Madhusudhan Rao was arrested in May 2025, while Anjaneyulu was secured on a Prisoner Transit Warrant for investigation.
The SIT examined 173 witnesses, and the investigation includes forensic reports, financial records, WhatsApp communications, electronic data, valuation records, videos and reconstruction of the evaluation processes at both the resort and Vijayawada.

A parliamentary panel has flagged a "drastic decline" in the number of schools and students as education level rises, noting that nearly 73% students drop out before finishing higher secondary.
The recommendation is part of the Tenth Report (Eighteenth Lok Sabha) of the Committee on Estimates (2026-27) on "Budget and Policy aspects for providing Affordable and Quality Education in the Country including Review of Central Board of Secondary Education", presented to Lok Sabha on Wednesday (August 12, 2026).
The committee noted that the number of schools at Secondary and Higher Secondary levels are very less when compared with the number of schools at Primary and Upper Primary levels.
It said as per the Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE) 2024-25, out of the total 10,92,671 schools, including all the government and government aided schools, there are 9,11,032 schools at primary level, 4,12,805 schools at upper primary level, 1,61,808 schools at secondary level, and only 90,866 schools at higher secondary level in the country.
With regard to the number of students enrolled, in primary classes there are 6,18,45,033 students and 4,08,93,978 students in upper primary classes from 6 to 8, which reduces to 2,36,68,220 in secondary, and further reduces to 1,64,17,949 in higher secondary classes.
Drastic decline in number of schools
"The committee are concerned to note this drastic decline in number of schools and students as education levels rises," it said.
"From the above information, the Committee note that out of over 1 million (10 lakhs) government schools, the vast majority are only primary schools, and nearly 73% of students drop out before finishing higher secondary," it added.
The committee strongly urged the Ministry to prioritise upgrading existing primary and secondary schools into full higher secondary schools to ensure a high school is physically accessible to students belonging to different communities and to arrest student drop-off rate.
"The Committee are of the view that there is an urgent need to increase the number of schools at secondary and higher secondary levels," it said.
Considering that education is placed in the Concurrent List of the Constitution with most schools under the jurisdiction of the State Governments and UT Administration, the committee desired the Ministry to impress upon all the State/UT Government to take steps for setting up of more secondary and higher secondary schools so as to increase the enrolment of students in the country.
Gap in the availability of CwSN friendly infrastructure
On facilities for Divyang students to achieve inclusive education across the country, the committee flagged a severe gap in the availability of CwSN friendly infrastructure, noting that more than half of schools across the country are devoid of CwSN-friendly infrastructure.
The committee noted that in order to achieve the objective of inclusive education, the Ministry of Education provides financial support to State Governments and Union Territories to strengthen infrastructure and human resources for inclusive education of Divyang students under the Samagra Shiksha scheme.
To improve physical accessibility of schools, the scheme includes specific provisions for the creation of barrier-free and differently-abled-friendly infrastructure, such as ramps, handrails and accessible toilets, so that children with disabilities can move safely and participate fully in school activities.
Though the committee appreciated the vision of the Ministry, it noted that as per UDISE+ 2024-25, out of total 14,71,437 schools at national level, only 5,23,143 schools have CwSN (Children with special needs) toilets, and only 8,08,466 schools have ramps with handrails.
During 2024-25, a budget of ₹482 lakh was allocated for construction of 186 CwSN toilets, however only ₹2.60 lakh was actually utilised with no progress in physical targets.
"The severe gap in the availability of CwSN friendly infrastructure shows that more than half of the schools across the country are devoid of CwSN friendly infrastructure," the committee said.
The committee further noted that under the financial support for new special educators, only ₹80.50 lakh was utilised against a budgetary grant (elementary section) of ₹962 lakh.
It also noted that a meagre progress was achieved in the area of recruiting/retaining special educators for CwSN students.
On the Ministry's approach to promoting education for Divyang children, the committee noted that it is rights based, inclusive and holistic.
It said The Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPnD) Act, 2016 provides that children with benchmark disabilities are entitled to free education up to the age of 18 years.
The NEP 2020 emphasises a Zero Rejection Policy for children with disabilities, ensuring that no child is denied schooling on account of disability. The policy also underscores the importance of preparing and training teachers to handle inclusive classrooms effectively, it said.
"In view of the above, the Committee strongly recommend the Ministry to adhere to yearly targets of budget utilisation and execution of CwSN related projects in a time bound manner," it said.
The committee recommended the Ministry provide safe and accessible infrastructure to Divyang students in a time-bound manner to achieve the objective of inclusivity in education.
The Ministry should also assess the requirement of special educators across the country and complete their recruitment at the earliest, it said.

On August 13, 1926, in the village of Birán in eastern Cuba, Fidel Castro Ruz was born. As the world observes his birth centenary this week, what strikes us most forcefully is not merely the memory of what Fidel did, but the weight of his absence. The centenary is being observed at a moment when that absence is immensely impacting the life and events of the world.
Consider the conjuncture. The Trump administration’s atrocities, its tariff wars against the developing world, its threats of annexation against sovereign nations, its gunboat menace in the Caribbean, its complicity and collaboration in the genocide of Palestinians and so on, are the vulgar and naked manifestations of imperialist domination in pursuit of a unipolar world. Against this offensive, the peoples of Asia, Africa, and Latin America are searching for a rallying voice. The absence of a leader of Fidel Castro’s stature, capable of uniting the Global South into a fighting force, is very much visible. That is precisely why his life must be studied afresh. Fidel was an incomparable world leader of revolution, and the different phases of his life, each of which left its impact on the lives of millions, deserve at least a brief survey.
From the ballot to Moncada
Fidel entered politics as a student activist at Havana University, where he was drawn into the turbulent anti-imperialist student movement of the late 1940s. His initial instinct was democratic and electoral; he wanted to contest elections to the Cuban House of Representatives in 1952 as a candidate of the Orthodox Party. History decided otherwise. On March 10, 1952, the U.S.-backed dictator Fulgencio Batista staged a coup d’etat, cancelled the elections and suspended the Constitution. Fidel first moved the courts against the usurper. When the courts predictably failed, he realised that no democratic election was possible under Batista, and he became convinced that the armed suppression of the dictator could be defeated only through armed struggle.
That conviction produced the assault of July 26, 1953, when Fidel led some 160 young rebels in simultaneous assaults on the Moncada barracks in Santiago de Cuba and the barracks at Bayamo. The attack did not succeed. Dozens of captured revolutionaries were tortured and murdered by Batista’s soldiery. Yet out of this military defeat Fidel forged a political victory that would change the hemisphere.
The genius of the Martí connection
Herein lies Fidel’s greatness: he could connect his project of revolutionary upsurge to José Martí, the apostle of Cuban independence. Martí can arguably be considered the greatest visionary of Latin American liberation; for Indian readers, he is best understood as Mahatma Gandhi, Bhagat Singh and Rabindranath Tagore rolled into one. A moral teacher of his people, a fearless fighter against colonialism, and a renowned poet whose verses are sung to this day, Martí was martyred in 1895 at the age of 42, fighting the Spanish colonisers on Cuban soil. He is revered as the father of the Cuban nation.
Put on trial after Moncada in fractured, secretive proceedings, Fidel, a lawyer by training, conducted his own defence. That defence is now known to the world as the ‘History Will Absolve Me’ speech. In it, Fidel declared that the intellectual author of the revolutionary liberation project of Cuba was José Martí. In the centenary year of Martí’s birth, 1953, the young rebels of Moncada called themselves the ‘centenary generation’. To connect a current event of historical significance to an epoch of the past, to make a nineteenth-century poet-martyr the living author of a twentieth-century revolution, is a remarkable act of political imagination. That was Fidel’s revolutionary genius. He understood that a revolution which cannot claim its national past will never win its national future.
Fidel and his fellow revolutionaries were sentenced to 15 years’ imprisonment. Such was the popular demand and upsurge across Cuba that Batista was compelled to release them in less than two years, under the amnesty of May 1955. The dictator believed he was releasing a spent force. He was releasing his own gravedigger.
Granma, Sierra Maestra, Revolution
Exiled, Fidel and his comrades travelled to Mexico, where they met a young Argentine doctor named Ernesto Che Guevara, beginning one of the great revolutionary partnerships of history. In November 1956, 82 fighters crammed into the small yacht Granma and sailed for Cuba. The landing was a disaster; only a small band survived to reach the Sierra Maestra mountains. From that remnant, in barely 25 months, Fidel built a rebel army that was rooted in the peasantry, won over the workers and students of the cities, and shattered a U.S.-armed military. On January 1, 1959, Batista fled, and the Cuban Revolution triumphed.
The significance of that victory cannot be overstated. The Cuban Revolution was successful, and it showed the world that a socialist country is possible even in the western hemisphere, right under the nose of U.S. imperialism, barely 90 miles from Florida. Washington understood this perfectly, which is why it responded with the Bay of Pigs invasion of 1961, decades of terrorism, and an economic war that continues to this day.
Tribune of the Three Continents
Fidel never conceived of the Cuban Revolution as Cuba’s private property. He became an inspiration and material support to liberation movements across Latin America and Africa. More than 300,000 Cuban volunteers served in Angola, where the 1988 victory at Cuito Cuanavale broke the back of the apartheid army and hastened Namibia’s independence and the fall of apartheid itself; Nelson Mandela travelled to Cuba in 1991 to say so in person. Cuban doctors and teachers went where imperialism sent only marines. Fidel provided outstanding leadership to the Non-Aligned Movement, hosting its 1979 Havana summit and chairing the movement twice, insisting always that non-alignment meant alignment with the oppressed.
When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 and triumphant ideologues proclaimed the ‘end of history’, Cuba lost the bulk of its trade overnight and entered the terrible Special Period. Fidel refused to capitulate. Even after the collapse of the USSR, he provided leadership for a socialist alternative, proving through Cuba’s survival that socialism was not a Soviet export but a people’s choice.
In these years, Fidel also widened the very agenda of anti-imperialism. He mainstreamed the analysis of new forms of imperialist exploitation, the debt trap, unequal exchange and neoliberal plunder, declaring already in the 1980s that the foreign debt of the Third World was unpayable and should not be paid. At the Rio Earth Summit of 1992, he warned, decades ahead of fashionable opinion, that an important biological species is at risk of disappearing due to the destruction of its natural habitat: humanity itself. And he argued forcefully that the former colonial powers owe reparations to their former colonies for centuries of colonial exploitation, a demand that today resonates from the Caribbean to Africa to our own subcontinent.
The system they could not kill
The CIA and its hirelings attempted to assassinate Fidel on more than 600 occasions, by the count of Cuban security. He overcame every one of them. Those attempts were never aimed at one man alone; the attempts to assassinate Fidel were attempts to murder the Cuban socialist system itself. Having survived them all, Fidel did what few leaders in history have done; he desired to make way for youngsters, voluntarily stepping down from responsibilities from 2006 and spending his final decade as a writer and counsellor of the Revolution until his death in November 2016.
The war on Cuba, however, did not die with its target. For over six decades, the United States has strangled the island through an illegal blockade, which Havana estimates has cost the Cuban economy more than 170 billion dollars, and which the UN General Assembly condemned yet again in 2024 by 187 votes to two. It is this strangulation, tightened further under Trump, that lies at the root of the economic and infrastructure crisis Cuba faces today. Cuba’s present hardships are not a verdict on socialism. They are a verdict on imperialism’s cruelty.
A hundred years after his birth, Fidel, Che and Cuba continue to inspire the world, especially Latin America and the Global South. In an hour when imperialism is again naked and vulgar, the centenary is not an occasion for nostalgia but a summons. The best tribute the workers, peasants and youth of India and the world can pay Comrade Fidel is to build the unity of the Global South and the struggle for socialism that his life embodied. History has absolved him. It is for us to vindicate him.
M.A. Baby is CPI(M) general secretary

Madhya Pradesh has received investment proposals worth ₹8,635 crore across various sectors during the Investment Dialogue held in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. These proposals are expected to create more than 5,785 employment opportunities. More than 500 industrialists, investors and corporate representatives from major industrial centres of Gujarat, including Ahmedabad, Surat, Bhavnagar, Rajkot and Vadodara, participated in the dialogue and expressed interest in investing in Madhya Pradesh. Chief Minister Dr. Mohan Yadav addressed leading industrialists and investors from across the country at the Mega Investment Dialogue— Interactive Session on Investment Opportunities in Madhya Pradesh — held in Ahmedabad on Wednesday, August 12, 2026.
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said Madhya Pradesh offers immense opportunities for business, setting up new industrial units, expanding existing ones and scaling up operations. Investment in Madhya Pradesh has always been a profitable proposition. Welcoming investors from across the country on behalf of the State’s 8.5 crore people, the Chief Minister said the State Government would provide every possible facility, security and support to investors.
The Chief Minister said, referring to the development drive underway across the country under Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi’s leadership to build a self-reliant India, Madhya Pradesh’s new industrial policies are receiving appreciation from the industry. He said, “For running an industry, what is primarily needed is a sound policy, good intent and a supportive government. You will find all three in Madhya Pradesh.”
Inviting Gujarat’s industry leaders to the upcoming Global Investors Summit-2027 in Bhopal, Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said, “You have the experience, and we have the opportunities. If our opportunities are combined with your experience, together we can create history.” He called upon industrialists to become partners in Madhya Pradesh’s growth journey and said, “Come, invest in Madhya Pradesh without hesitation and with an open heart, and become part of this historic journey of development.”
Land, power and water: No concern for investors
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said investors in Madhya Pradesh need not worry about electricity, water or land. Industrial land is available on lease at concessional rates, the State has adequate water reserves and surplus power, and plug-and-play zones are being developed. As many as 48 new industrial parks are being developed across nearly 19,000 acres. The Chief Minister said, describing the single-window system as “end of problems, instant service,” that solutions to every hurdle are available on a single digital platform. Highlighting seamless connectivity as a major strength of Madhya Pradesh, he said the State has a road network of more than 5 lakh kilometres, strong rail connectivity, eight airports, six inland container depots, expressways and highways. He added that trained and skilled manpower is also readily available in the State.
Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat are twin brothers
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said, highlighting the industrial potential and scope for high-quality mutual cooperation between Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, the two States are like twin brothers. Gujarat brings technological expertise, business acumen and industrial experience, while Madhya Pradesh offers abundant water resources, a large land bank and a strategic logistics advantage due to its central location. Combining these unique strengths can create a new chapter of industrial development in the region.
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said Madhya Pradesh offers vast opportunities for Gujarat’s petrochemical, chemical, textile, pharma, food processing and automobile sectors. The large petrochemical refinery in Bina, the state-of-the-art Medical Device Park being developed over 360 acres in Ujjain, PM MITRA Parks in Dhar and Navsari, and the strong automobile base in Pithampur further strengthen the prospects for industrial cooperation between the two States. He said Madhya Pradesh has received investment proposals worth more than ₹34 lakh crore across various sectors over the past two and a half years, of which investments worth more than ₹10 lakh crore have already been grounded. Policies related to renewable energy, pumped hydro and biomass have facilitated investments, with ₹7.19 lakh crore invested in these sectors.
“Two sons of Maa Narmada advancing together for industrial growth”
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said the land of Gujarat has contributed to the country’s prosperity since the era of Lord Krishna. Gujarat has given the nation great personalities such as Mahatma Gandhi and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel. Today, under Prime Minister Shri Modi’s leadership, India is moving towards becoming a leading nation in the world. He said Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh are like two sons of Maa Narmada. The waters of the Narmada are providing adequate drinking and irrigation water to both States. Prime Minister Shri Modi has fulfilled his commitment to the Sardar Sarovar Dam. Conditions are becoming increasingly favourable for both States to advance in industries, business, culture and other sectors. The Chief Minister said entrepreneurship and business create employment and livelihood opportunities for many people. He said, “We are people who move forward on the principle of ‘live and let live.”
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said, welcoming industrialists and entrepreneurs attending the Mega Investment Dialogue, that the relationship with Gujarat dates back to the time of Mahatma Gandhi. All States jointly participated in the freedom struggle, while Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel from Gujarat played a key role in laying the foundation of modern India. The Chief Minister said Lord Krishna received his education in Madhya Pradesh and later became Dwarkadhish and Jagadguru in Gujarat. He said Gujarat is the land that bestowed the honorific “Shri” upon Krishna and brought prosperity. The Chief Minister said a new chapter of relations between Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh is now emerging, inviting entrepreneurs from Gujarat to establish industries in Madhya Pradesh and assuring them of full government support. He said Gujarat has immense potential in petrochemicals, chemicals, textiles, pharma and energy. Gujarat’s textile industry is renowned globally. Prime Minister Shri Modi laid the foundation stone of the PM MITRA Park being developed over 2,000 acres in Dhar district, where investments are rapidly coming in. The Chief Minister added that Prime Minister Shri Modi is also from Gujarat and, under his leadership, India is creating a distinct global identity.
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said coordination between Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat is rapidly increasing, reflecting Prime Minister Shri Modi’s vision of prosperity for the States. Emphasis has been laid on necessary cooperation between the States in the context of the Sardar Sarovar Project. Adequate guidance and support from the Centre have been available to both States during Prime Minister Shri Modi’s tenure. The environment is becoming increasingly favourable for mutual cooperation and balanced growth across various sectors.
Industry-friendly policies and positive investment environment
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said the State Government has implemented robust policies for industrial development. Special efforts have been made in the renewable energy sector, and Madhya Pradesh has surplus power availability. Electricity generated in Madhya Pradesh is also powering metro trains in Delhi. He said Madhya Pradesh offers among the lowest electricity tariffs in the country.
The State Government has created a positive investment environment by implementing industry-friendly policies. He said investment incentives promised to investors have been paid to large industries and MSME units up to the previous month. The Government has also cleared the backlog of subsidies through its commitment to investors.
Chief Minister Dr. Yadav said, extending greetings on Youth Day, that opportunities are being created for youth to advance in every sector in Madhya Pradesh. The State has immense potential in tourism, IT and food processing. The Government has resolved to develop metropolitan cities in Indore-Ujjain and Bhopal by integrating neighbouring districts. He said medical colleges and industries are being established in Madhya Pradesh at a rapid pace. The State has one of the lowest unemployment rates in the country. The Chief Minister also highlighted the State’s initiatives in renewable energy, investments across various sectors, and industry-friendly policies that are creating a positive investment environment.
Gujarat entrepreneurs share positive experience of investing in Madhya Pradesh
Shri Chintan Thakkar, owner of Gujarat-based Welspun Transformation Services Limited, shared his experience of investing in Madhya Pradesh. He said Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh are not only sister States but also future growth engines of the country. Shri Thakkar said that his company entered Madhya Pradesh in 2011 and established a unit on the Dewas-Bhopal Road to manufacture water pipes. The Madhya Pradesh Government granted all necessary approvals for establishing the industry within just 12 months. He said that under the leadership of Chief Minister Dr. Yadav, the government is fulfilling its financial commitments to entrepreneurs and investors.
Additional Chief Secretary, Industrial Policy and Investment Promotion Shri Neeraj Mandloi apprised investors of Madhya Pradesh’s strengths. He said neighbouring Gujarat has always inspired the country through its entrepreneurship, ability to overcome challenges and innovation. He said Madhya Pradesh has a land bank of more than one lakh acres for industrial development. Eight airports, 22 railway junctions and rapidly expanding logistics corridors provide strong connectivity. The State Government has planned eight dedicated industrial parks, including a Footwear Park in Morena, a Medical Device Park in Ujjain and a Plastic Park in Raisen. He said sector-based clusters are a key strength of Madhya Pradesh. NITI Aayog has recognised Madhya Pradesh as a leading State in framing investment promotion policies. The State’s industry-oriented policies are also being adopted by other States. These policies promote exports and investment incentives.
Madhya Pradesh is set to host the Global Investors Summit in January-February 2027. The State is the country’s largest wheat producer and third-largest milk producer, ensuring adequate availability of raw material for food processing. Pithampur has the country’s largest automobile testing track. The country’s largest PM MITRA Park for the textile sector is being developed in Dhar district, with investments worth more than ₹2,000 crore already received.
Madhya Pradesh’s Ease of Doing Business policies are supporting investors across sectors. New industrial parks are being developed in Bhopal, Jabalpur and Ujjain. With support from the Central Government, the country’s first Telecom Manufacturing Zone (TMZ) is being developed in Gwalior. Tourism will become one of the biggest sources of employment in the future, he said, adding that Madhya Pradesh is a leading State in wildlife and religious tourism. The State Government is providing all possible support to entrepreneurs investing in the tourism sector. Principal Secretary, Science and Technology Shri M. Selvendra said Madhya Pradesh has immense potential for growth in the IT sector. Indore, Bhopal, Gwalior and Jabalpur offer world-class facilities at lower costs than those in other States. The cost of living is also relatively low.
TCS operates a unit in Indore employing more than 16,000 people, while Infosys is also planning to expand its operations in the State. Compared to Bengaluru and Hyderabad, Madhya Pradesh offers much easier traffic conditions. The State Government is working to establish a new Space Tech Park. A green zone is also being developed in Bhopal for drone manufacturing infrastructure and drone testing. Under the Space Tech Policy, the Madhya Pradesh Government provides capital subsidies of 40% to 60%. The State’s Semiconductor Policy is receiving a positive response nationwide. The State Government is also providing support towards rent and staff salaries for setting up industries.
Shri Achal Bakeri, CMD of Symphony Limited and Chairman of Confederation of Indian Industry’s Gujarat State Council, said Madhya Pradesh is the heartland of Incredible India. The State has set new benchmarks in tourism in recent years, with more than 14 crore domestic tourist visits recorded. He said Madhya Pradesh is now emerging as a leading destination for domestic tourism alongside traditionally popular destinations such as Goa and Himachal Pradesh. The Karnataka Legislature’s monsoon session will begin on August 13 with an ignominious first in recent history: a Cabinet with not even a symbolic representation of women.
The last fortnight has been marked by endless squabbles over Cabinet expansion and portfolio allocation, with intense arguments on ways to ensure caste and regional representation. Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and party functionaries have made multiple trips to New Delhi to consult with the high command, and spent much energy trying to placate “powerful” leaders who are miffed over being denied Cabinet berths or over not getting what are described as “plum portfolios.”
However, women’s representation has clearly not been regarded as an issue worth breaking a sweat over. When asked by the media why not a single woman was included in his 33-member Cabinet, Mr. Shivakumar candidly admitted that there was “no urgency” in the matter, while casually assuring that the one vacant place would be filled by a woman. In fact, it was in an equally casual manner that Gayathri Shanthegowda, the lone woman who was in the Congress high command’s approved first list of Ministers, disappeared before the swearing-in ceremony, as the urgent demands of other powerful interest groups took over.
This situation is nothing short of ironic for two reasons: Congress has nationally been vociferously arguing for 33% women’s reservation, without encumbering it with delimitation or any other riders. At the State level, the Congress government has come to power riding on the back of five guarantees, two of which are specifically aimed at women’s empowerment. While the Gruha Lakshmi scheme promises ₹2,000 a month to women heads of eligible families, Shakti offers free travel to women in select buses.
Symbolic representation
The signalling is that while women are very crucial as voters, they are the last priority when it comes to sharing political power. The final electoral rolls published ahead of the 2023 elections showed that women voters outnumbered men in 17 electoral divisions out of the 34 in Karnataka. Naveddu Nilladiddare, a network of feminists and women’s rights groups, in a letter to the Chief Minister, put it succinctly: “An all-male Cabinet is not an oversight. It is a political choice. It sends an unmistakable message that women and women’s leadership remain dispensable when it comes to the exercise of state power.”
Interestingly, while there have been multiple street protests by supporters of leaders demanding their induction into Cabinet — foregrounding their caste, region, seniority etc. — there were hardly any protests against the non-inclusion of women in the Cabinet. There was some feeble noise in Belagavi in north Karnataka over Lakshmi Hebbalkar, who handled the Women and Child Development portfolio under the Siddaramaiah-led government, being dropped, but none on the larger question of women’s representation. Brahmins not being represented in the Cabinet grabbed more attention than women being denied a place.
The history of electoral politics in Karnataka shows that women’s share in political representation has always been abysmal, much like the rest of the country. In the 2023 Assembly elections, out of a total of 2,613 candidates, 185 were women. Of them, 10 were elected (with one more added in bypolls), which constitutes about 4.5% of the total Assembly strength. In the first two elections in Karnataka in 1957 and 1962, the share of women’s representation stood at 6.25% and 8.65%, respectively, the latter being the highest ever. Since then, the share has fluctuated, with the 1972 election seeing not even a single woman elected to the Assembly out of the 28 who contested. This is all the more striking in a State which was a pioneer in giving 50% reservation to women in local bodies.
The representation of women in Ministry too has been symbolic across parties, with the highest being four when the late S.M. Krishna was the Chief Minister. Women are often given what are regarded as “light weight” portfolios such as Women and Child Development or Kannada and Culture.
No doubt Mr. Shivakumar will stick to his promise of filling the one vacant berth with a woman, but that will not go beyond what it has always been — a symbolic gesture — in the absence of a system that makes representation count.

Inside a dark room at Luz’s MdnD performance space, the laughs are on. As the Tamil theatre group Crazy Creations stage their evergreen comedy play, ‘Marriage Made in Saloon’, the entire first row erupts in laughter at a clever wordplay that its protagonist, ‘Maadhu’ Balaji, has just cracked.
This could be a Sunday evening at any of the leading sabhas in Chennai. Except it is not.
Here, the audience is so close to the performer that — in Balaji’s own witty words — “kai romba neetina, yaara mooka kuthiduven” (If I stretch my hand too much, I’ll poke the nose of the person in the first row”).
With about fifty people watching, seated close to each other and to the performers, late playwright Crazy Mohan’s Tamil comedies are not only finding new audiences but also a home in intimate spaces in the city. Through ‘Chamber of Humour’, Crazy Mohan’s brother and actor, Madhu Balaji, wants to take Tamil theatre to smaller sets of audiences.
“A friend of mine (RK Ramanathan, Carnatic vocalist Ramnad Krishnan’s son) recently spoke about how ‘Chamber of Music’ would happen in the past,” recalls Balaji. “Leading Carnatic vocalists would perform at someone’s house to select audiences. This would be followed by a discussion on the song list and the ragas featured in it. I thought it was a fantastic idea that Tamil theatre could borrow.”
Helping him implement the idea that most of Crazy Mohan-driven plays relied primarily on dialogue and wordplay. “Our productions don’t have elaborate backdrops or lighting. It is like a duet between the artiste and the audience.”
Up close and personal
It helps that the artiste is just a few feet from you, feels Kalyanasundaram K of MdnD, which will be hosting a line-up of plays for the next few months and during the season of Margazhi. “You almost relate to the person speaking on stage. It is the equivalent of staging a play in your hall.”
Apart from relatability, such a setting also allows you to let your guard down. Explains Balaji, “Before the play, we tell audiences to have no inhibitions. Our aim is to see them laugh heartily, which in turn spurs us on to deliver our lines better.”
Slowly, ‘Chamber of Humour’ will be spreading to other areas in Chennai; Balaji is currently scouting for small venues in places like Shenoy Nagar and Ambattur, where the same troupe once staged many of their plays. “We are ready even if a terrace is available!”
Beyond this concept, Balaji is also looking at ways to bring some of Mohan’s scripts to life. “There are two that stand out for me — one called Madhu MLA and another titled Son of Superman. Apart from that, he has also penned many dialogues or scenes that do not belong to a particular play. We wish to stitch them together to form a storyline.”
Helping him in this pursuit to carry the comedian’s legacy forward is popular actor Kamal Haasan. “He (Kamal) is a big supporter and has taken on a mentoring role,” states Balaji. “He tells us that just like there is patronage for his comedy films like Michael Madana Kama Rajan and Avvai Shanmukhi, there will be audiences for the plays too.Upon his advice, we are also roping in several youngsters, even for key roles. That way, we hope to carry Crazy Mohan’s legacy to the next generation.”
‘Chamber of Humour’ will next be staged on September 13 (Madhil Mel Maadhu at 4 pm, followed by Chocolate Krishna at 6.45pm) at MdnD performance centre, Luz Church Road

“Experiences of harassment and discrimination were reported across several settings. Some 91.8% of respondents reported verbal harassment at least rarely, while 52.5% reported physical threats or violence at least rarely. Among valid responses, 85.0% reported discrimination in school or college at least rarely, and 63.2% reported workplace discrimination,” it said.
The survey also found that 72.9% of valid respondents felt compelled to change their behaviour or appearance sometimes or more often to retain work or education. A further 57.9% said their identity affected access to employment or income opportunities at least rarely.
Religious, cultural exclusion
“Mental wellbeing emerged as a significant concern. Among valid responses, 76.7% reported experiencing stress, anxiety or emotional distress related to discrimination sometimes or more often, including 48.3% who experienced it most of the time or always. Access to mental-health or peer support was uneven: 41.0% said such support was available most of the time or always, while 36.1% said it was available rarely or never,” the report said.
The findings also point to a gap between awareness of rights and confidence in institutions. While 56.7% of valid respondents agreed that they were aware of their legal rights, 63.3% disagreed that laws and policies adequately protect LGBTQIA+ persons, and 66.7% disagreed that police and authorities respond sensitively to LGBTQIA+ issues.
Religion, culture and social belonging received particularly cautious assessments. Some 72.1% did not agree that religion or faith practices are accepting of LGBTQIA+ persons. More than half disagreed that their identity is compatible with their cultural or tribal background or that local traditions allow space for diverse identities, with 51.7% of valid respondents disagreeing that they feel a sense of belonging in society.
Healthcare emerged as a comparatively more positive area. Among valid respondents, 56.7% said that they felt comfortable accessing healthcare most of the time or always, and 75.0% said healthcare providers treated them with respect most of the time or always.
“Friends were the most frequently reported source of support, mentioned by 37 respondents, followed by LGBTQIA+ networks, mentioned by 12.
Six respondents mentioned. Awareness and sensitisation were the most common single priority identified for improving LGBTQIA+ lives in Arunachal Pradesh, followed by legal protection,” the report said.
HRI director Ranju Dodum said the study was intended to begin building locally grounded evidence on experiences that are often discussed without adequate data.
“LGBTQIA+ experiences in Arunachal Pradesh cannot simply be assumed from national conversations. Family, community, tribal identity, religion, education and employment all shape how people experience acceptance and safety here. This is a baseline study and its numbers must be read with methodological caution, but they point to questions that deserve deeper research and serious public discussion,” he said.
The report recommends sustained sensitisation programmes in schools, colleges, workplaces, healthcare institutions, police and public administration; confidential mechanisms for reporting discrimination; stronger mental-health and peer-support systems; safe community spaces; more inclusive education and workplace practices; and locally grounded engagement with families, community institutions and faith leaders.
The survey sample was predominantly young, with 90.2% of respondents between 18 and 35 years.

The Greater Chennai Corporation’s (GCC) property tax reassessment drive has drawn heavy backlash over sharp increases and a lack of prior consultation and transparency.
A GCC official said the revised tax was based on self-declared property area. The first revision was carried out in 2018, followed by a major one in 2022, but the collection was subsequently paused. The revised rate should have been collected 2022 onwards, and is now being implemented, he said.
T.K. Shanmugam, chairman of the Federation of North Chennai Residents’ Welfare Associations (FNCRWA), said a resident, who had been paying a property tax of ₹295, was demanded ₹3,255 following the reassessment, without receiving any explanation. Mr. Shanmugam said the residents were not given details such as the rate per square foot or the basis for the revised assessment.
He further questioned whether the residents would be able to approach the Revenue Department officials to raise objections, given the large number of properties involved.
He said many houses in North Chennai had undergone additions over the years that may not have been reflected in earlier assessments. However, he criticised the manner in which such changes were being reassessed using only drone and GIS-based methods, without manual confirmation.
Many also took to social media, saying the sudden move and close deadline had put several residents between a rock and a hard place.
Sandhya Vedullapalli, secretary of the Federation of Anna Nagar Residents’ Associations, said that for her, the tax was revised from ₹895 to ₹1,835 — a 100% increase. She alleged that in an apartment complex, only one flat had received the reassessment notice, raising questions about uniformity in the exercise.
For Vijaykumar, who owns a space in Mogappair, the rate went up from ₹6,500 for six months to over ₹31,000, nearly a five-fold increase. “I am yet to raise an objection. Such sudden increases could affect businesses, especially small ones,” he said.
‘Received information’
Meanwhile, Tiruvottiyur CPI(M) councillor R. Jayaraman said several residents in his ward had received information regarding the revision.
He said the GCC had taken the decision without passing a resolution in the Council. “There was no prior information. When there is an online gateway to register complaints about all issues, there ought to be one for this too. We will put forth our objection in the next Council meeting,” Mr. Jayaraman said.
Pointing out that the earlier property tax increases had contributed to public dissatisfaction with the previous regime, CPI(M)’s G. Selva said the new government should reconsider the decision.
Some residents of Thoraipakkam and Neelankarai had received information about the revision, A. Francis of Thoraipakkam Residents’ Welfare Association said.
Buffer zone
Kumararaja of Velachery said some residents of Tansi Nagar, Annai Indira Nagar, Vijay Nagar, Mahatma Gandhi Street, and Nehru Street had received reassessment notices.
He said the properties in these localities had been classified as having “zero value”, as they fell within the buffer zone of the Pallikaranai marshland. Since further development was not possible in the area, he questioned the basis for revising the property tax, and said the decision should be reconsidered.
A resident of Nanganallur said: “The GCC has increased the tax for the apartment owned by my bedridden mother. From the earlier half-yearly rate of ₹900, the tax has now been revised to ₹3,300. The property is held exclusively by my mother aged 80. As she has been bedridden since last year, her family pension is not adequate to meet the mounting medical expenses. Either the basic street rate should be reduced or it should be reduced on a par with core areas of Chennai. Nanganallur has higher rates than some core areas,” he said.
Arun, a resident of Adambakkam, welcomed the move, saying it corrected under-assessed properties rather than imposing a uniform hike. Though he agreed that a reassessment of under-valued properties would increase revenue for the GCC, he said there should have been greater transparency and awareness among the public.
Chairman of the Standing Committee on Taxation and Finance Sarbajaya Das told The Hindu that the decision had been taken by the Commissioner and the Deputy Commissioner (Revenue and Finance).
She said the reassessment had initially been intended for commercial buildings, followed by around 6,000 residential properties. The committee had not been informed that residential properties would also be reassessed under the new government, she said.
Stating that the Council had not been informed that objections could be raised, Ms. Das said they would demand a portal to address the issue and greater transparency at the next meeting of the Standing Committee on August 23 or 24.
She added that the GCC was facing a severe fund crunch, with no maintenance or ward development funds released and a liability of ₹2,000 crore.
GCC’s response
The GCC has issued notices to three lakh assessees for under-assessment of property tax. It expects to generate an additional revenue of ₹83 crore per annum from the revision of property tax on under-assessed properties.
Corporation Commissioner G.S. Sameeran, in a statement, said: “The change is only for properties that were under-assessed and those that were converted to commercial. It is based on GIS, satellite imagery, other government databases, and the owner’s self-declaration of area. The assessee can request remeasurement and reconsideration to RDCs. The same will be disposed of within a month,” he said.

Meta says it has taken down 756,000 Australian teen accounts as ban enforcement looms
The Australian government proposed the landmark law, which came into force on Dec 10, on concerns about social media's impact on the physical and mental health of children and young teens.
SYDNEY: Facebook and Instagram owner Meta said on Thursday (Aug 13) it had taken down more than 750,000 accounts it suspected were held by Australians aged under 16 since a world-first ban on teen accounts, and promised more action in the face of possible regulatory intervention.
The company said it had deactivated 462,000 suspect Instagram accounts and 294,000 suspect Facebook accounts from just before the Australian social media ban went live in December to June, up from 331,000 Instagram accounts and 173,000 Facebook accounts it said it had removed by January.
The world's largest social media company has said it wants to comply with a law it and other platforms have vocally opposed, just as Australia's internet regulator considers an enforcement lawsuit against platforms, including some that Meta owns, that it says have failed to take sufficient steps to comply with the law.
No other platforms have released compliance data that matches the date range given by Meta, but Australian government figures and multiple independent studies have shown more than eight in 10 under-16s were still on social media in the ban's first three months.
The Australian government proposed the landmark law, which came into force on Dec 10, on concerns about social media's impact on the physical and mental health of children and young teens.
With other countries around the world considering similar age-restrictions, Australia has accused the platforms of intentionally setting the ban up to fail, and has introduced a law to double the maximum penalty for non-compliance to A$99 million (US$69.75 million) and give the regulator greater document discovery powers.
PARLIAMENTARY HEARING ON FRIDAY
Representatives of Meta, TikTok, YouTube owner Google and Snap's Snapchat are scheduled to give evidence in a parliamentary inquiry about the changes on Friday, as are regulatory and government officials.
"Enforcement is ongoing, and these numbers will continue to grow," Meta said in a statement.
"We share the Australian Government's goal of ensuring young people have safe, age-appropriate experiences online, and we are meeting our obligations under the law," the company added.
A 2025 Australian trial of age assurance technology found products on the market could effectively support a ban.
Most large platforms, including Meta's, rolled out photo-based age estimation software, although they say they typically first subject users to age inference, or assuming a person's age based on their online activity.
Meta said it was using AI to analyse user profiles for "contextual clues that an account may belong to someone under 16, such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades" and to analyse reports about suspected underage accounts.
The company added that it had removed the option for a person to make more attempts to set up an account if their previous account was deleted.
