On National Librarians Day, a garlanded photograph of S.R. Ranganathan stands in the first-floor corridor of the State Central Library. A little further down, about a dozen readers sit hunched over their books. The whizzing sound of spray-painting echoes through the heritage building, which has been under repair for three years. “The work has been inconsistent. At times it moves quickly, and then at other times it slows down. We are disappointed with the pace,” says a library official, unwilling to speak on record.
“I come here to study but sit in this shaded area because it is quiet. I bring my own books as the library mostly has textbooks and not the study material I need,” says Ziyan, a resident of Tadbund preparing for the NEET examination.
He spends much of his day studying under a tin shed erected at the rear of the 1936 building. Several other aspirants preparing for competitive exams also use the space. Most bring their own study material, saying the library does not have the resources they need. The library has a collection of more than five lakh books, including nearly two lakh in English.
The State Central Library’s patronage has declined over the decades due to poorly organised books, staff shortages and a lack of basic amenities. The conservation work that began three years ago was expected to bring a turnaround, but the library is yet to see the anticipated improvement.
Inside, the foyer and the librarian’s desk are covered in paint and lime stucco, as are the stained-glass panels. The main hall has been cleared for conservation work and has remained that way for nearly a year. “Most of the English books section has been closed and is inaccessible. We keep moving the shelves around depending on the requirements of the work,” the library official says.
Beyond the ongoing repairs, the library is also grappling with a chronic shortage of staff. “There are 104 sanctioned posts, but we have only 33 regular staff, including officers, besides 16 outsourced employees and nine junior assistants who were recruited last year after the Congress government came to power. We are still short-staffed and cannot maintain the library properly,” the official says. The post of chief librarian is also vacant.
The library functions under the State government, with the bulk of its expenditure going towards salaries. According to the revised estimates for 2025-26, a total ₹4.35 crore has been earmarked for salaries, while only ₹8.21 lakh has been budgeted for other expenses. The limited allocation for maintenance is reflected in the condition of the facilities. The heritage building has hosted film shoots for decades, with Sita Ramam being among the more recent big-budget productions to shoot extensively at the location. Today, however, its surroundings are cluttered with an RTC logistics counter, Annapurna canteen, a makeshift pavement shelter and dozens of private buses parked outside the building.

The Tamil Nadu Forest Department has sought an ownership certificate and other documents from individuals for possession of a Lar Gibbon, after a video of actor Vikram playing with and hugging the animal went viral and drew backlash.
Yogesh Kulal, Wildlife Warden, Chennai, said the animal has since been moved to Erode from businessman C.K. Ranganathan’s residence in Injambakkam.
The Lar Gibbon (Hylobates lar) is listed in Appendix I of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES). Its import requires the requisite CITES import and export permissions, Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) documentation and permission from the Chief Wildlife Warden of the State to which it is being imported.
Sources said the trail of the Lar Gibbons can be traced to Erode and, before that, to Manipur. As per records, a Manipur-based stockholder, Laikhuram Singh, declared eight Lar Gibbons — four males and four females — in 2020 under the declaration of stock of exotic live species through PARIVESH 1. The records identify Malaysia as their country of origin.
A subsequent Form I under the Living Animal Species (Reporting and Registration) Rules, 2024, records the transfer of three Lar Gibbons — one male and two females — from Mr. Singh in Manipur to S.K. Keshavanathan in Perundurai, Erode for adoption.
K.V. Appala Naidu, District Forest Officer, Erode, said a male and a female gibbon were found on the premises and Mr. Keshavanathan informed that he had applied for possession of three gibbons, but one animal had died earlier. “We need to verify if the animal actually died or if there was an undocumented transfer,” he said.
According to sources, Mr. Ranganathan is said to have obtained the animals from Mr. Keshavanathan. However, the transfer certificate is yet to be approved by authorities.
Chief Wildlife Warden Rakesh Kumar Dogra said the department was examining the circumstances under which the animals reached Tamil Nadu and whether all statutory requirements governing their possession and transfer had been complied with.
Wildlife and animal welfare activist Antony Clement Rubin said keeping primates as pets could increase the risk of zoonotic disease transmission, particularly at a time when animal-to-human spillover of pathogens is being increasingly documented.
He also said a celebrity of Mr. Vikram’s stature posting a video of himself interacting with a Lar Gibbon could fuel demand for such vulnerable animals, which are trafficked through illegal wildlife networks.

From seven deceased donor organ donations in its first year, to 266 in a single year, Tamil Nadu has come a long way in 17 years. Behind the rise is a gradual shift in public perception, shaped by sustained awareness efforts, measures to build confidence, and trust and improvements in the State’s transplant infrastructure and systems.
The numbers tell a compelling story of how far the State has come with regard to organ donation and transplantation. Since 2008, the highest number of deceased organ donors was recorded in 2024, when Tamil Nadu had 268 donors. In 2025, there were 266 donors - 211 men and 55 women. A total of 1,476 organs were utilised - 856 major organs and 620 minor organs and tissues that year, according to the Transplant Authority of Tamil Nadu’s data.
On World Organ Donation Day, which falls on August 13, experts revisit the milestones, the lessons learnt and the road ahead.
How it worked
J. Amalorpavanathan, founder-member secretary, Transplant Authority of Tamil Nadu, said, “When we started in 2008, the concept of brain death was scarcely understood among healthcare professionals. A few coordinated brain death certifications were happening sporadically, with MOHAN Foundation [an NGO] coordinating around two to three such cases a year in a few city hospitals. The State government had decided to start the Cadaver Transplant Programme (CTP), and the groundwork began in April. We went on to issue 10 government orders. It was in September that year that the parents of 15-year-old Hithendran (who had sustained severe injuries in a road accident and was declared brain dead) decided to donate his organs. The CTP was launched in October 2008, and Hithendran’s case helped organ donation pick up in the State.”
Recalling his visits to all districts, he said that initially, there was reluctance among doctors. “But whenever I interacted with the general public, I found a sense of receptiveness. In fact, though they had questions and sought clarifications, I found the least resistance among them. We slowly convinced healthcare professionals to certify brain death. We had seven donations in the first year, and crossed 180 in a year in eight years. Though the number of organ donations dipped during the COVID-19 pandemic, it picked up again thereafter,” he pointed out.
Families coming forward
Sunil Shroff, managing trustee of MOHAN Foundation, said there had been a tremendous improvement in awareness levels over the years. “Earlier, we found it hard to obtain consent for organ donation. Now, many families are coming forward to donate. In States such as Tamil Nadu and Telangana, where awareness is relatively high, I think that 10 to 15% of families come forward to donate. This is a paradigm shift,” he observed.
About 72% of deceased organ donations in the country happens in five States - Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka. Southern states, he said, have done well in terms of creating awareness on organ donations.
Compared with other States, awareness about organ donation was far higher in Tamil Nadu. Unpublished data from a major transplant centre showed that the acceptance rate was 70 to 75% after the first counselling and increased by another 10% following the second counselling, a senior doctor noted.
“According to me, awareness creation can be approached in two ways. One is to organise awareness campaigns and sessions and encourage people to take pledges. In T.N.’s experience, we found that news about successful donations, honour walks for donors and giving due recognition to donors were more effective awareness tools. Since October 2023 (the former DMK government issued an order to accord State honours to the mortal remains of deceased donors in September 2023), more than 800 such State honours have been accorded. News about successful donations and the utilisation of donated organs has proved to be a more effective way of creating awareness,” Dr. Shroff explained.
What’s needed now
Dr. Amalorpavanathan said that the involvement of people and healthcare professionals along with government support has helped improve organ donation in the State. “Successive governments did their best to take the programme forward. We have well developed infrastructure and doctors who are willing to go the extra mile,” he said.
However, this brings in another perspective. “We have an unacceptable number of brain deaths due to the high number of road traffic accidents. We need to reduce accidents and make roads safe. Developed countries have moved towards Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD), and we should also explore this possibility. In living donor organ transplants, we should promote swap transplants in a big way,” he noted.
At a recent press conference on a heart transplant in a young patient with Dilated Cardiomyopathy, Rajeev Thilak Chellasamy, heart transplant surgeon at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, elaborated on DCD. He noted that India has a long waiting list for transplants, and has traditionally relied on donations following brain death, while DCD was not ethically approved in the country. In DCD, the practice of which has been around for nearly 10 to 15 years, the heart is connected to a perfusion system. DCD numbers have increased in North America. If considered, it is a viable opportunity to increase the pool of donor hearts. The number of people dying while on the waiting list has increased and this needs to be addressed, he said.
Dr. Shroff called for establishing green corridors in hospitals for seamless integration of organ donation processes so that there are no missed opportunities. Similarly, every hospital should have nodal officers in place, he said.

With this registration, Nexent Capital is authorized to undertake a broad range of investment banking activities permitted under the CMI Regulations, including managing initial public offerings (IPOs), follow-on public offerings (FPOs), SPAC listings, secondary listings, depository receipt issuances, debt capital market transactions, and other capital market advisory mandates within GIFT City's regulatory framework.

It enables us to help international companies access global capital through GIFT City while strengthening India's position as a global financial centre. We look forward to supporting innovative, high-growth businesses as they leverage GIFT City's evolving capital markets ecosystem."
The registration comes as GIFT City continues to strengthen its position as a gateway for global capital markets, offering international companies an alternative venue to access investors through India's IFSC ecosystem. Leveraging its newly acquired license, Nexent Capital plans to expand its cross-border investment banking platform by supporting high-growth companies, particularly from the United States and Europe, seeking capital-raising and listing opportunities through GIFT City's exchanges.

No backdoor entry: Supreme Court gets UPSC assurance on Odisha DGP selection
The UPSC told the Supreme Court it will not finalise recommendations for Odisha’s next DGP until the court hears a plea challenging the selection process.
The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) on Thursday assured the Supreme Court that it would not convene a meeting to finalise its recommendations for the appointment of Odisha’s next director general of police (DGP) until the court hears a challenge to the state government’s move to expand the pool of officers being considered for the post.
The undertaking came after a bench headed by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant indicated that it was inclined to restrain the UPSC from making any fresh selection until the matter is heard on August 18.
“Any backdoor entry is not acceptable…UPSC must not finalise till the next date of hearing,” the bench, also comprising justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, said.
The court’s intervention followed an application alleging that the Odisha government was attempting to circumvent the Supreme Court’s prescribed procedure for the appointment of DGPs by introducing officers who were not part of the original list of three senior-most eligible officers sent to the UPSC.
Senior advocate P Chidambaram appeared for the petitioner.
Also Read: Odisha DGP selection delayed amid procedural, integrity concerns
The controversy comes days before incumbent DGP YB Khurania, a 1990-batch IPS officer appointed as Odisha’s police chief on August 16, 2024, is due to demit office on August 16.
Under the procedure laid down by the Supreme Court in its 2006 judgment in the Prakash Singh case, states are required to send proposals of eligible officers to the UPSC, which prepares a panel of three officers from among those meeting the prescribed criteria. The state government is then required to appoint the DGP from that panel.
The plea alleges that the Odisha government initially forwarded the names of three senior officers -- Sudhanshu Sarangi, a 1990-batch IPS officer, and Susanta Kumar Nath and R P Koche, both from the 1993 batch, for consideration by the UPSC.
However, before the UPSC could take a call on the three names, the state is alleged to have expanded the list to 11 officers by adding eight IPS officers from the 1994 to 1996 batches.
The issue gained significance after the Odisha government on August 10 promoted two 1994-batch IPS officers, Sanjeeb Kumar Panda and Yeshwant Kumar Jethwa, to the rank of DGP. The petition alleges that their elevation could bring them into consideration if the original list of three officers is replaced or expanded.
The UPSC’s empanelment committee was expected to meet in New Delhi on Thursday to shortlist three officers for the post, a day after the PIL was mentioned before the Supreme Court.
On August 11, Chidambaram had told the CJI-led bench that the state was attempting to breach the procedure prescribed in Prakash Singh.
“The State of Odisha is breaching the Prakash Singh judgment. On August 7, the UPSC was scheduled to meet to select from among the three DGPs. Odisha withdrew the list. They are now making another list to send,” he had submitted.
The senior counsel had alleged that the state was attempting to promote an ADGP and include the officer in the fresh list of candidates for consideration.
The CJI had then pointed out that under an earlier Supreme Court order, the UPSC was duty-bound to approach the court in case of non-compliance with the prescribed directions.
The Supreme Court reiterated in February 2026 that states must adhere to the procedure laid down for the appointment of DGPs. Under the framework, the UPSC is required to prepare a panel of eligible officers, following which the state government must appoint the police chief from among those empanelled. The court has also made clear that prescribed eligibility criteria cannot be bypassed merely because the number of eligible officers is limited. The DGP post at Level 17 is to be filled through selection from among officers holding DGP-level posts at Level 16.
The Prakash Singh judgment, delivered in 2006, had laid down a series of measures aimed at insulating the police from political interference and improving professionalism and accountability in policing. The procedure for selection of state police chiefs was among the key safeguards prescribed by the court.

Ex-Punjab deputy CM Sukhbir Singh Badal attacked with 'kirpan' outside gurdwara in Maharashtra's Nanded
Former Punjab deputy chief minister Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked near Nanded Sahib gurdwara on Thursday.
Shiromani Akali Dal president and former Punjab deputy chief minister Sukhbir Singh Badal was reportedly attacked by a Nihang at Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur on the outskirts of Nanded, Maharashtra, on Thursday. Badal sustained an injury to his hand and was rushed to a nearby hospital for treatment.
The incident took place around 15 km from the main Gurdwara Nanded Sahib, one of the five Takhts, or temporal seats, of Sikhism. Badal was reportedly heading towards the langar hall after paying obeisance at the gurdwara when he was attacked with a kirpan.
The gurdwara is controlled by a Nihang samparday and is not managed by the board that oversees the main Nanded Sahib gurdwara. Following the attack, Badal was shifted to the nearby Yashosai Hospital.
A viral video following the incident showed Badal walking inside a building with a saffron-coloured cloth wrapped around his right hand.
Badal had arrived in Nanded on Wednesday with his family and a group of close associates as part of a three-day visit. He was inside the gurdwara with his wife, Harsimrat Kaur Badal, a Shiromani Akali Dal MP.
BJP spokesperson RP Singh condemned the attack, calling the incident “completely unacceptable” and saying that violence has no place in a democratic society.
In a post on X, he wrote, "Punjab and the Punjabi community have already suffered immensely during the dark and painful years of violence and militancy. Generations of Punjabis have borne the deep scars left by that period. We cannot, under any circumstances, allow those dark days to return. Peace, brotherhood, constitutional values and the rule of law must always prevail.
I pray for the good health, safety and speedy recovery of S Sukhbir Singh Badal Ji."
2024 assassination bid

Messi event row: Kerala CM flags GST fraud, lapses in picking private sponsor
Kerala CM VD Satheesan stated that a preliminary inquiry report submitted by the sports department is being examined and warrants further investigations
Kerala chief minister VD Satheesan on Thursday flagged serious charges, including Goods and Services Tax (GST) fraud and lapses in the way the private sponsor was picked by the previous Left Democratic Front (LDF) government in connection with the cancelled visit of the Lionel Messi-led Argentina national team to play a friendly in the state.
The chief minister stated that a preliminary inquiry report submitted by the sports department is being examined and warrants further investigations.
“What was the procedure adopted in selecting a private firm to sponsor the event? Was there an Expression of Interest? A firm was picked, but parameters including its source of funding and financial capability were not considered. Did the previous government know about this? There are already a lot of contradictory statements coming out,” the CM said at a press briefing in Thiruvananthapuram.
He said that the finance department, which he oversees, will take action and make efforts to recover the state’s losses in GST collection.
“Prima facie, GST fraud has taken place. There are some serious allegations. It happened during the tenure of the previous government and even a notice was served (to the private sponsor). But it seems the inquiry was frozen,” he said.
On whether central agencies will be invited to probe aspects of possible money laundering, the CM said,
“Let the state government examine it first. If there is a need for central agency probes, we will refer it to them. Have the State’s interests been protected? Did the private firm take advantage of the situation? Everything will be examined.”
The CM also rejected allegations made by a top official of the private firm that the state government was targeting the firm.
“The inquiry report has just been submitted to me. I have not taken any action on it,” he said.
In 2023, then sports minister V Abdurahiman had announced that the state government was partnering with RBC to host the Messi-led Argentine side to play a friendly exhibition match at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Kochi at no cost to the public exchequer. However, the event failed to materialise.

Abdurahiman and the private firm have rejected the allegations made in the inquiry report.

As soon as the House met for the day, all six stanzas of the national song were played, following which Speaker Om Birla adjourned the House sine die (for an indefinite period).
Mr. Birla did not read out the usual valedictory address in which he highlights the performance and productivity of the Lok Sabha during the session.
Parliament Monsoon Session highlights
Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah and Defence Minister Rajnath Singh were present when the House met for a brief while.

On Thursday (August 13, 2026) too, the Opposition raised slogans against the government.
The session began on July 20 and witnessed vociferous protest by the Opposition earlier over the NEET paper leak issue and alleged theft of donations at the Ram temple in Ayodhya.
Later, the Opposition demanded a response from Home Minister Amit Shah over the police crackdown on students at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi on July 20. The students were protesting against the NEET paper leak and seeking accountability in the education system.

Though the House could not complete the Question Hour on any of the days due to opposition protests, as many as 12 Bills were passed, including two earlier cleared by the Rajya Sabha.

The Foreign Contributions (Regulation) Amendment Bill, which had become a sticking point between the government and the opposition over some of its provisions, was on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) referred to a joint committee of Parliament for threadbare discussions.
The Bill was introduced in the Budget session but was not moved for consideration and passage as several religious organisations had opposed it, including those from Kerala where Assembly polls were due in April.
As the Opposition questioned Mr. Shah’s absence from the House proceedings, he hit back by urging Speaker Birla on Wednesday to consult the Opposition for a debate on students' protests over the NEET paper-leak issue and said he is ready to answer all questions in the House.
In a letter to the Speaker, Mr. Shah said dialogue and discussions are the only ways to find solutions in a democracy and he has full faith in democracy and democratic institutions.
On the penultimate day of the session, the report of a probe panel constituted by the Speaker to investigate charges of wrongdoing against Justice Yashwant Varma was tabled in Parliament. Varma has been found guilty by a panel, with the committee saying the charges of unexplained cash, disturbing evidence and evasive explanation against him "are proved".
In view of this, the government may go ahead with the impeachment (removal by Parliament) process against the judge in the Winter session of Parliament, sources said.

Lok Sabha passes bill restricting states’ power to tax minerals amid protests
The bill, which amends the Mines and Minerals (development and regulation) Act, 1957, was introduced on Monday by minister of coal and mines G Kishan Reddy.
The Lok Sabha on Wednesday passed the Mines and Minerals (development and regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, which aims to restrict state governments from imposing taxes, cesses or levies on minerals rights and ‘mineral-bearing lands’, via voice vote sans debate amid opposition protests.
The bill, which amends the Mines and Minerals (development and regulation) Act, 1957, was introduced on Monday by minister of coal and mines G Kishan Reddy. It was passed in the second half of the Lok Sabha session on Wednesday, with Jagdambika Pal, who was in the chair, beginning proceedings by asking the Opposition to maintain decorum.

The amendment bill introduces a new section that says that “no tax, cess or such other levy (by whatever name called) shall be imposed by the state Government on mineral rights; or mineral bearing lands, either based on mineral quantity or mineral value or royalty payable…except in accordance with such conditions or restrictions as may be prescribed by the Central Government..”
The bill also proposes to expand the central government’s powers to regulate mines to mineral bearing lands having ore content in accordance with the parameters prescribed under the MMDR Act.
The proposed amendments are the fallout of a July 2024 ruling by the Supreme Court that upheld the power of states to levy taxes on mineral rights and and mineral-bearing lands.

Kerala Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan on Thursday (August 13, 2026) said the State government would mount strong political and, if necessary, legal opposition to the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, passed by the Lok Sabha a day ago.
He said the legislation amounts to “a serious encroachment on the State’s constitutional powers over land and poses a grave threat to India’s federal structure.”
Addressing mediapersons after the Cabinet meeting, Mr. Satheesan said the State’s principal objection was that the proposed amendment seeks to bring powers relating to land, a domain that comes under Entry 18 of the State List of the Indian Constitution, within the Centre’s sphere of authority.
He pointed out that the Constitution clearly distributes legislative powers between the Union, State and Concurrent Lists. While the Union has legislative authority over matters in the Union List, States have exclusive authority over subjects in the State List, and both have powers over subjects in the Concurrent List. Land, he pointed out, falls under Entry 18 of the State List and therefore comes within the legislative jurisdiction of the States.
He alleged that the Centre was attempting to expand its jurisdiction through the definition of “mineral-bearing land”, without even excluding coastal areas and forests. The State government will formally convey its protest to the Centre. It would also consider legal remedies if the Bill is ultimately passed and becomes law.
Vizhinjam port to begin EXIM cargo movement
Mr. Satheesan announced that direct export-import (EXIM) cargo movement at the Vizhinjam International Seaport will begin on August 18.
Vizhinjam has thus far been handling transshipment operations alone. Around 60% of the containers handled there have been containers originating from or destined for other countries.
The commencement of direct EXIM cargo movement will mark the first major milestone towards ensuring that the State begins to receive the direct economic benefits of the international port.
The Customs Commissionerate has already issued the necessary public notices for the commencement of EXIM cargo movement, he said.
A temporary road connection from the port road to national highway 66 has also been completed in accordance with the directions of the National Highways Authority of India. This arrangement has been put in place to facilitate cargo movement between the port and the national highway.
Mr. Satheesan added that the absence of an existing Container Freight Station facility in Thiruvananthapuram has necessitated an arrangement within the port itself. A Customs-bonded area has therefore been established inside the port, and the related work is progressing.
Aid for Wayanad landslide victims
The Cabinet also decided to provide an additional ₹2 lakh in financial assistance to all beneficiaries included in the Mundakkai-Chooralmala landslide rehabilitation list. He said the measure had been proposed earlier and that the government had now decided to implement it fully, with an expenditure of over ₹5 crore.
The Cabinet also decided to proceed with signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) required for implementing the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana - Urban (PMAY-U) 2.0 through the Local Self-Government Department.
The Chief Minister informed that the Centre has placed certain conditions for the signing of the agreement. Among them is a requirement concerning the use of an emblem or logo associated with the scheme.
He said while there was no requirement to display a photograph of the Prime Minister, a logo or emblem specified as a condition by the Centre would have to be accepted when the MoU is signed.
The government has also issued guidelines for providing the bonus for the 2025-26 financial year to employees of public-sector institutions in Kerala.

The Karnataka bandh called by Kannada organisations on August 13 over the Cauvery water issue received a lukewarm response in Bengaluru and several parts of the State, with normal life largely unaffected.
The bandh was scheduled from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., but public transport and commercial activity continued as usual in Bengaluru. A team of police officers visited the residence of the former MLA and took him into custody. When officers attempted to speak to him, Mr. Nagaraj reportedly refused to respond and instead tied tape around his mouth, indicating that he was observing a silent protest.
The bandh was called by certain groups to protest against the directive to release Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu at a time when Karnataka is reeling under drought-like conditions following poor rainfall.
Little response in other parts of State
In Mysuru city, shops and commercial establishments remaining open and schools and colleges functioning normally. KSRTC buses and autorickshaws also operated as usual.
Barring symbolic protests by pro-Kannada activists and moral support from sections of the trade and business community, normal life remained largely unaffected by the muted response to the shutdown call.
Hotels and restaurants remained open, and normal activity was witnessed across the city. Businesses on busy commercial hubs D. Devaraja Urs Road and Sayyaji Rao Road functioned without any disruption.
As a precautionary measure, police personnel were deployed in sizeable numbers in the central business district to prevent any untoward incident.
Some pro-Kannada activists and members of the Cauvery Action Committee were taken into preventive custody when they attempted to block buses at the Sub-Urban Bus Stand. Farmers under the banner of State Sugarcane Growers’ Association, led by Bhagyaraj, marched on the streets carrying empty pots. Karnataka Kavalu Pade and other pro-Kannada groups staged a symbolic protest at Sri Jayachamarajendra Circle in protest against the directive to release water.
KSRTC Mysuru Rural Division Controller Veeresh said bus services were being operated normally despite the bandh. “All scheduled services are being operated, with passengers being ferried to their destinations without any disruption,” he said.

The story so far: The Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) chairperson Saumitra Kumar Haldar has called for the establishment of a river board that will “own, operate, manage, and regulate” reservoirs in the entire Cauvery basin to resolve the vexatious dispute between Tamil Nadu and Karnataka over the sharing of the water resource.
In essence, he favoured the idea of treating the Cauvery river as one unit and managing its resources accordingly, instead of going by political boundaries of territories through which the river flows.
What is a river board?
A river board is a body of officials and specialists who approach the river concerned as a single hydrological unit and deal with the issues of utilisation, management, protection, improvement, and sustainable use of water resources across the river basin.
In Australia, the Murray–Darling Basin Authority, one of the widely discussed river basin organisations internationally, also studies complex connections among climate, river flows, and river-related outcomes for communities, industries, and the environment.
In 1956, when the re-organisation of States on linguistic lines was carried out and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act was formulated for adjudication of inter State river water disputes, the country came out with the River Boards Act. Under this law, the Union government, when approached by a State government or otherwise, can establish such an organisation for advising the State governments interested in relation to such matters concerning the regulation or development of an inter-State river or river valley or any specified part thereof.
How many river board bodies have been set up under the 1956 law?
None.
However, river boards and commissions have been constituted through the Union government’s resolutions and executive orders; laws based upon interstate agreements or states’ re-organisation, and awards of tribunals.
As the successive governments at the Centre had realised that the River Boards Act remained only as a dead letter, they had been mulling over replacing the law with legislative measures such as the River Basin Management Act and the permanent inter-State river water disputes tribunal law.
M. S. Menon, veteran water expert and former Member-Secretary of the Indian National Committee on Irrigation and Drainage, in an article in The Hindu on August 30, 2009, criticised the Union government for not promoting the idea of inter-State cooperation in this regard and taking the stand that “‘water’ is a ‘State subject,’” whenever confronted with water disputes among the States.
Also read | A year on, no headway in implementing river boards’ purview
Which are the river board bodies that have been established, independent of the River Boards Act?
- Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC) - Constituted in July 1948; States concerned: West Bengal and Jharkhand
- Tungabhadra Board - Formed in October 1953; States concerned: Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana.
- Bhakra Beas Management Board - Originally established as Bhakra Management Board in October 1967 and later acquired the present title in May 1976 with the merger of the Beas Construction Board (BCB); States concerned: Haryana, Rajasthan, Himachal Pradesh, and Punjab
- Betwa River Board - Constituted in 1976; States concerned: Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh.
- Narmada Control Authority - Established in December 1980; States concerned: Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Rajasthan
- Upper Yamuna River Board - Set up in March 1995; States concerned: Himachal Pradesh, Haryana Uttarakhand, Rajasthan, and National Capital Territory of Delhi
- Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards (two bodies) - Formed in May 2014; States concerned: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
- Cauvery Water Management Authority - Established in June 2018; States concerned: Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry.
- Mahadayi PRAWAH (Progressive River Authority for Welfare And Hannony) - Constituted in May 2023; States concerned: Goa, Karnataka and Maharashtra
What has been the experience of intra-State river boards?
Not encouraging.
Tamil Nadu, in January 2001, constituted Palar and Tamiraparani River Basin Management and Development Boards. Headed by the Public Works Minister, the Boards included offiiials and three representatives each from industry and NGOs, including eminent persons in the respective areas.
The bodies were to take all decisions regarding the development and management of water resources in the two basins. Barring holding a few meetings, the two boards became defunct in due course of time.
Kerala’s Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala, as Mavelikara’s Member of Parliament In April 2002, called for the constitution of a river basin authority to acilitate the smooth implementation of the Pampa River Action Plan for pollution abatement and conservation. Two years later, at an event organised in Palakkad by the Centre for Water Resources Development and Management (CWRDM), Kozhikode, a strong demand for the formation of the Bharathapuzha River Basin Authority was made for integrated management of land and water resources.
In August 2021, Water Resources Minister Roshy Augustine told the Kerala Assemblly that a river basin management plan would be prepared for the Bharathapuzha. But, not much was heard about the plan since then.
How has the failure of the River Boards Act been handled by experts bodies in recent years?
The Commission on Centre State Relations (2010), headed by former Chief Justice M.M. Punchhi, analysed the issue and pointed out that the reasons for this had generally been ascribed to the “reluctance of States to politically come to an understanding.”
The Commission, while recommending a standing tribunal for all inter-State river water disputes, had also suggested the establishment of inter-State River Boards charged with an integrated watershed approach towards inter-State rivers. It also made it clear that any reference to the proposed tribunal should be invariably linked with the river boards and the initiating party must indicate the efforts made by it in resolution of its grievances before the river board in question.
What is the way forward?
The Union government’s attempt to amend the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, by providing for a single tribunal with different benches along with fixation of strict timelines for adjudication, has not been successful.
If the Centre announces a huge package of financial assistance for inter-State river boards, there is every chance that the States may evince interest. It can take the initiative to this effect at zonal council meetings.

Delhi court flags ‘criminal breach of trust’ by 3 experts in NEET-UG paper leak
A Delhi court said three subject experts accused in the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak prima facie committed criminal breach of trust with the NTA.
A Delhi court has observed that three subject experts accused of leaking the NEET-UG 2026 question paper prima facie committed criminal breach of trust with the National Testing Agency (NTA), which had engaged them to translate the examination paper after they undertook not to disclose its contents.
The observation was made by Fast-track court special judge Ajay Gupta of Rouse Avenue Courts while taking cognisance of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)’s 20,000-page chargesheet filed earlier this month against 13 people in the alleged NEET-UG 2026 paper leak case.
The court order specifically focused on the role of PV Kulkarni, a Chemistry subject expert, in “taking advantage” of the lack of an adequate security apparatus at the NTA’s headquarters to leak the question paper.
“It prima facie seems from the chargesheet that A-2 (PV Kulkarni) was fully aware that there was no practice of frisking of the subject experts at the designated place, therefore, he took advantage of the situation and took along with him chits/short notes prepared by him discreetly while doing the translation work for his subject,” it said.

The court said that the three subject experts, Kulkarni for Chemistry, Manisha Mandhare for Biology and Manisha Havaldar for Physics, had clearly given an undertaking before the translation work that they would not divulge examination-related material to anyone else.
“This prima facie shows that these accused persons have committed the criminal breach of trust with the NTA authority which engaged them for the purpose of translation of NEET (UG) 2026 exam question paper of their respective subjects,” the court observed.
The judge further underlined how the questions were leaked through the subject experts and subsequently travelled to students through intermediaries.
“...it is also prima facie clear from the record that all these subject experts, in active conspiracy with other co-accused persons, have in order to obtain the illegal monetary gain, sold the exam related material to the co-accused persons as well as several candidates in the guise of providing coaching to them,” it said.
The court also noted that the accused persons disposed of the leaked questions and destroyed their electronic devices in order to hide evidence, thereby making them liable to be prosecuted under the relevant sections of the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.

“It is prima facie clear from the overwhelming incriminating material collected by the CBI through an extensive investigation that all the accused persons, in one manner or the other, formed part of NEET (UG) 2026 Exam leak syndicate and each one of them have played an active role in the dissemination and circulation of the exam question paper of all three subjects,” the court said.
The matter is now at the stage of scrutiny of documents and has been listed for arguments on charge to begin from next week.
The CBI had earlier this month filed a chargesheet against all 13 arrested accused in the alleged NEET-UG 2026 question paper leak case, saying its investigation had traced the leak from the paper setters to the beneficiary candidates and uncovered the entire chain of the alleged conspiracy.
The chargesheet invokes charges of criminal conspiracy, cheating, criminal breach of trust, destruction of evidence, and offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act and the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.
The agency said it has relied on 360 witnesses, 422 documents and 43 material objects to support the prosecution. All 13 charge-sheeted persons are currently in judicial custody.
Among those charge-sheeted are three subject experts contracted by the National Testing Agency (NTA) to set the Chemistry, Biology and Physics papers, several alleged middlemen and two persons linked to coaching institutes.
According to the chargesheet, no government official, including any office bearer of the NTA, was involved in the leak. Investigators concluded that the question paper was leaked by teachers contracted to set the examination.

Canadian wildfire that forced 20,000 to flee may signal ‘new normal’
British Columbia Premier David Eby says a fast-moving wildfire in western Canada that forced more than 20,000 people from their homes may signal a “new normal” after outpacing official models and giving some residents little time to evacuate
PENTICTON, British Columbia -- A wildfire that forced more than 20,000 people from their homes in western Canada moved so quickly that crews had to abandon firefighting to help residents escape, a pace British Columbia’s premier said Wednesday may represent a “new normal.”
The Bald Range wildfire erupted Friday near Summerland, a community of about 12,000 in British Columbia’s Okanagan region. By Wednesday, it had grown to about 184 square kilometers (71 square miles) after destroying homes and killing an 80-year-old woman.
"There’s an important set of lessons for us to take about how quickly this moved and that this may be our new normal for fire speed," Premier David Eby said. He said the blaze outpaced wildfire modeling and left some residents with little time to evacuate.
Officials have begun damage assessments, but the area remained unsafe Wednesday and there was no timeline for residents to return.
Crews were clearing vegetation to help slow the fire’s spread as officials warned that thunderstorms could bring erratic winds and increase fire activity. Highway 97, a major route through the area, remained closed.
Eby visited an evacuation reception center in Penticton, where he said he met people devastated by the loss of their homes.
“A lot of emotions in there, obviously,” he told reporters, calling the woman’s death a “tragic loss.”
Summerland pharmacist Jonathan Kiesman said he was worried about displaced patients getting their medications and said seeing the fire approach the community “almost brought tears to my eyes.”
Officials said they were withholding broader details on property losses until residents could be notified directly.

“The last thing that I would want is somebody to have the shock of finding out on social media or on television about their home being lost,” British Columbia Emergency Management Minister Kelly Greene said.
Eby said the province would review the response, including whether changes are needed to wildfire planning, building standards and vegetation management near communities.
Given the drought and summer heat, he warned, “this is very unlikely to be the last significant fire we see this summer.”
Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes warned that recovery would be long and difficult.
Canada has endured a series of severe wildfire seasons in recent years, with smoke repeatedly drifting into the United States. In record-setting 2023, fires burned more than 14.6 million hectares (36 million acres), an area roughly the size of Illinois.
Canada has warmed faster than the global average in recent decades, while the amount of land burned by wildfires has increased substantially. Much of the country’s forest is remote and dominated by spruce and pine, conditions that can make fires difficult to contain once they become established.

A first-of-its-kind multidisciplinary programme brings global standards of lymphatic care to India, shifting the focus from reactive treatment to prevention for women at risk of cancer-related lymphedema
NEW DELHI , Aug. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Apollo Athenaa, Asia's first dedicated women cancer centre by Apollo Hospitals, today announced the launch of India's first one-stop comprehensive Lymphedema Clinic, accredited by the Lymphatic Education & Research Network (LE&RN) —an internationally recognised non-profit organisation dedicated to advancing education, research and advocacy for lymphatic diseases—setting a new benchmark in the management of cancer-related lymphedema. Designed around internationally recognised standards of care, the clinic brings together specialised surgeons, lymphedema therapists, nurses, dermatologists and rehabilitation experts under a single multidisciplinary programme, offering comprehensive care spanning prevention, early diagnosis, advanced microsurgery, rehabilitation and lifelong follow-up.
The Apollo Athenaa Lymphedema Clinic is distinguished by its integrated model of care, combining multidisciplinary clinical expertise, advanced imaging and supermicrosurgical capabilities, specialised rehabilitation, and internationally benchmarked protocols to deliver personalised care with superior clinical outcomes and an enhanced quality of life for patients. Patients have access to dedicated lymphedema assessment, manual lymphatic drainage, complete decongestive therapy, compression therapy, stage-specific rehabilitation, lymphovenous bypass surgery, vascularised lymph node transfer and liposuction for selected advanced cases. The programme is further strengthened by ultra high-frequency ultrasound technology, enabling surgeons to accurately identify lymphatic vessels and veins for performing lymphatic bypass procedures with greater precision.
India is estimated to have over one million people living with lymphedema. Of these, an estimated 400,000–600,000 are living with cancer-related lymphedema, with 30,000–50,000 new cases developing annually. As cancer survival rates continue to improve, this burden is expected to rise, underscoring the urgent need for dedicated multidisciplinary lymphedema services.
Women undergoing breast and gynaecological cancer treatment remain among the most vulnerable, as lymph node removal and radiation therapy can permanently disrupt lymphatic drainage, resulting in chronic swelling, recurrent infections, reduced mobility and a significant impact on long-term quality of life. Up to 20% to 42% of women develop arm lymphedema after breast cancer surgery, and roughly 31% to 37% of survivors of gynecological cancers experience lower-limb lymphedema. Despite this growing burden, access to specialised multidisciplinary lymphedema care remains limited in India, with patients often navigating fragmented treatment pathways that delay intervention and compromise long-term outcomes.
Dr. Preetha Reddy, Executive Vice Chairperson, Apollo Hospitals Group , said, "At Apollo, we have always believed that advancing healthcare means continually raising standards across every stage of the patient journey. As cancer outcomes continue to improve, our focus must also extend to helping patients live healthier, fuller lives beyond treatment. Apollo Athenaa, Asia's first dedicated cancer centre for women, was created with this vision of delivering comprehensive, women-centric cancer care. The launch of India's first LE&RN-accredited Lymphedema Clinic is a natural extension of that commitment. By bringing together specialised expertise, advanced technology and internationally recognised standards of care within a multidisciplinary programme, we are addressing an important aspect of survivorship that has often been overlooked, while ensuring women receive the highest quality of care throughout their recovery."
Dr. Venkat Ramakrishnan, Consultant Plastic & Breast Reconstruction Surgeon, Apollo Athenaa , said, "Traditionally, lymphedema surgery has largely been considered only after the condition develops, when irreversible tissue changes may have already occurred. At Apollo Athenaa, we are changing this paradigm by introducing a preventive approach through Prophylactic Lymphovenous Bypass (LVB) for eligible patients undergoing cancer surgery who are at high risk of developing lymphedema. Performed at the time of axillary lymph node dissection, this super microsurgical procedure restores lymphatic drainage during cancer surgery itself, helping reduce the future risk of arm lymphedema rather than waiting for the condition to manifest. This shift from reactive treatment to preventive lymphatic surgery has the potential to significantly improve long-term outcomes and quality of life for women undergoing breast cancer treatment."
Dr. Samarth Gupta, Senior Consultant Plastic & Breast Reconstruction Surgeon, Apollo Athenaa , said, "Lymphedema care cannot be delivered in isolation. It requires timely diagnosis, specialised rehabilitation, precision surgery and long-term follow-up working together as one coordinated programme. At Apollo Athenaa, we have brought together every aspect of lymphedema care—from dedicated assessment and specialised physiotherapy to advanced imaging, microsurgical reconstruction and survivorship support—under one roof. By combining evidence-based protocols with technologies such as high-frequency ultrasound, we are able to deliver highly personalised care while helping patients regain function, confidence and quality of life."
With the launch of the LE&RN-accredited comprehensive Lymphedema Clinic, Apollo Athenaa continues to strengthen its women-centric oncology ecosystem by advancing survivorship care through integrated prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and long-term follow-up. By bringing globally benchmarked standards of lymphatic care to India, the centre aims not only to improve long-term functional recovery and quality of life for women living with or at risk of cancer-related lymphedema, but also to enable them to return to their everyday lives with greater confidence, dignity and well-being- reflecting Athenaa's commitment to care beyond cure.
ABOUT APOLLO ATHENAA
Apollo Athenaa, a unit of Apollo Hospitals Enterprise Ltd, is Asia's first dedicated cancer centre for women, rooted in empathy and powered by science. It is not just a facility—it's a mission. Apollo Athenaa is envisioned as a safe, specialised space exclusively for women, combining cutting-edge oncology expertise with compassion, dignity, and privacy. Women are the cornerstones of families and communities, and their health directly impacts the strength of the nation. Recognising the need for timely, specialised, and compassionate care, Apollo has taken a pioneering step forward. Apollo Athenaa provides comprehensive women-focused cancer care, from preventive screenings and advanced diagnostics to surgical oncology, breast oncoplasty, fertility preservation, and reconstructive care. Supported by multidisciplinary expertise and precision oncology, the centre also offers nutrition, physiotherapy, onco-psychology, and palliative care, ensuring a continuum of services that place women's health, dignity, and well-being at the forefront.

Artificial intelligence may be changing the way we think about creativity, but a new exhibition at Bikaner House shows that technology is not replacing the artist; it is simply giving artists another medium through which to express themselves. For instance, Riyas Komu, who is known for hyperrealistic portraits, has done a digital work showing the time of Mahatma Gandhi’s death — 5.17pm on January 30, 1948.
Riyas is one of nine major contemporary artists who have stepped beyond the familiar worlds of paint, stone, and bronze to explore digital fine art in (Re)claiming Rights of Render(ing), presented by NewArtX (NAX).
Apart from Riyas, the show features works by Alex Davis, Atul Bhalla, Gigi Scaria, GR Iranna, Sibdas Sengupta, Teja Gavankar, Vibha Galhotra, and Waswo X Waswo. The artists have employed virtual reality, interactive installations, digital sculpture, video art, and projection technologies to present ideas that remain deeply rooted in each artist’s existing practice.
For Saryu Pareek Gupta, co-founder, NewArtX, the exhibition is less about showcasing technology and more about creating an ecosystem where artists can experiment with it. “The artists conceptualised these works because they felt the digital medium was the best way to express their ideas. Our studio team supports them with the technology, software, and hardware needed to realise those concepts,” explains Saryu.
NewArtX is a Mumbai-based studio led by Saryu and Pulkit Gupta that offers tech support to artists who are keen on exploring the digital medium. Founded in May 2024, the studio has presented three shows till now, but this is its first conceptual solo show.
Manan Shah, curator of the show, pointing at Vibha Galhotra’s work Who Owns The Earth? shares that the viewers will be transported to a desert upon wearing a VR headset, where they will be put in an uncomfortable space and asked tough questions. Vibha continues with the theme of climate change in the work, but instead of a sculptural installation, she has done an interactive installation. “It’s a conceptually strong show,” adds Manan.
Manan says that the participating artists were selected not because they already worked with technology but because they were keen on extending their idea to a new format. Alex Davis, known for sculptural installations, has a fascination for metal. “He brings the same luminescence in this digital sculpture too,” remarks Manan.
As for the other artists, Teja Gavankar has created an interactive installation, whereas Gigi Scaria uses digital tools to manipulate images before transforming them into collages and sculptural forms. Atul Bhalla and Sibdas Sengupta employ video walls and digital editing to create moving-image works centred on environmental and social concerns, while Waswo X Waswo and GR Iranna combine photography, digital editing, and fine-art printing to build layered visual narratives.
According to Pulkit, the objective of NewArtX is to remove the financial and technical barriers that often prevent artists from working digitally. “We want to create an ecosystem for artists who want to explore the digital medium and support them through a digital studio, technology, and hardware so they don’t have to bear the financial burden of producing these works.”
(Re)claiming Rights of Render(ing) is on view at LTC, Bikaner House, New Delhi, until August 14.

Heavy rain lashed Odisha for the last 24 hours as the low-pressure area in the Bay of Bengal has become "well marked", the IMD said on Thursday (August 13, 2026).
The IMD has issued a “red warning” (take action) of very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across Odisha.
The national weather agency in its morning message said, "The well-marked low-pressure area over North Bay of Bengal and adjoining Bangladesh-West Bengal coast moved northwestwards. It is likely to continue to move northwestwards across Gangetic West Bengal towards Jharkhand and may concentrate into a depression during the next 12 hours."
A depression is a weather system stronger than a low-pressure area but less intense than a tropical cyclone.
While issuing the “red warning” of very heavy to extremely heavy rainfall across Odisha on Thursday (August 13), the IMD said that Gangetic West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand would also be impacted by the ongoing wet spell caused by a low-pressure system in the Bay of Bengal.
Keeping in view the weather conditions, the IMD has advised fishermen not to venture into the North Bay of Bengal and along the Odisha-West Bengal-Bangladesh coast till August 14.
According to the Meteorological Centre (MC), Bhubaneswar, the highest rainfall of 236mm has been recorded at Bhograi in Balasore district, followed by 230mm at Shyamakhuntam 215mm at Baripada in Mayurbhanj district and 204mm at Rajghat in Balasore district.
Balasore town recorded the highest rainfall of 137mm by 5.30 a.m. on Thursday (August 13), while reports of very heavy rains were received from Similipal Hills in Mayurbhanj. The very heavy rains in Mayurbhanj led to a rise in the water levels of rivers such as Budhabalanga and Jalaka in Balasore district. A large part of Balasore town has been encountering waterlogging, an official said.
Meanwhile, in the wake of the heavy rainfall since last night (August 12), the authorities declared the closure of all educational institutions in Mayurbhanj district on Thursday (August 13).
A district administration notification said that all headmasters, headmistresses, principals and teachers should attend their respective schools as usual to disseminate information about the closure to all students and their parents/guardians through available communication channels, including class WhatsApp groups, phone calls and SMS.
The Meteorological Centre Bhubaneswar said that under the impact of the low pressure, wind speeds along the Odisha coast could reach 30 to 40 kmph. Residents are advised to remain alert during thunderstorms and lightning and follow weather advisories issued by the authorities.

The students’ protest over alleged irregularities in Jharkhand recruitment examinations entered its 20th day on Thursday (August 13, 2026), with the agitators refusing to call off the stir until their demands were met.
Also read | For Jharkhand’s job aspirants, it was a march for lost years
The ‘JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch’ has been demonstrating at the Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in Ranchi, demanding greater transparency in recruitment examinations, cancellation of several tests and an independent probe by the CBI or a panel of retired judges from outside Jharkhand.
Former Chief Minister Raghubar Das on Wednesday (August 12, 2026) threatened to proceed on a hunger strike if the demand for a CBI probe was not fulfilled in a week, while the ABVP has announced protests at more than 1,200 universities over the issue.
Mr. Das also sought ₹1 crore each in compensation for the families of 19 people who died during the 2024 excise constable physical examination.
ABVP leaders have questioned the credibility of the state-appointed SIT into the alleged irregularities, citing repeated changes in its composition.
The BJP has accused the Hemant Soren government in Jharkhand of suppressing the movement, while the Congress criticised the saffron party of politicising the students’ agitation and claimed it brought workers from outside the State to disrupt the protests.
Tensions rose after a confrontation between protesters and the police during their march towards the assembly on Monday (August 10), with security personnel using batons, water cannons and tear gas to disperse the agitators.
The BJP subsequently observed a statewide bandh over the police action.
Meanwhile, JLKM leader Devendra Nath Mahto, who has been on a hunger strike and is undergoing treatment at a hospital after his health deterioated, sought permission from the Ranchi civil surgeon to return to the protest site, saying his “soul” remained with the students’ movement.
Four students on hunger strike were also receiving treatment at hospital.
Earlier, six rounds of talks between the government and student representatives failed to end the deadlock.
Chief Minister Hemant Soren has maintained that his government is committed to recruitment exam reforms and assured protesters the 14th JPSC examination would be cancelled, while accusing the BJP of using the agitation for political gains.
